590	volume was matched for the two protocols (i.e., 3/7 vs. 4x6) (129).
591	Subsequently, we examined the relative contributions of neural and muscular adaptations to the
592	gains achieved by the elbow flexors after a 12-week (2 sessions/week) training program with a
593	load of 70% of 1RM performed by moderately trained individuals (130). Training involved a total
594	 of ~50 repetitions in each session in an attempt to optimize the dose/response (see 17). The 3/7
595	protocol was repeated twice with a 150-s rest between the two bouts and compared with the 8x6
596	method; 150 s of rest between sets. Our results indicated that both protocols (3/7 and 8x6)
597	increased the 1RM load (22.2 vs. 12.1%; p<0.05) and MVC force during an isometric contraction
598	(15.7 vs. 9.5%; p<0.05) with a greater increase in 1RM load (p<0.05) and marginally greater
599	MVC force (p=0.07) for the 3/7 method.
600	 D
601	The EMG activity of two elbow flexors (long head of biceps brachii and brachioradialis),
602	 EP
603	normalized to their respective maximal M wave (Mmax) elicited by supramaximal electrical
604	stimulation of the motor nerve, increased (p<0.05) with no difference between training methods
605	 TE
606	(14.5 vs. 8.1%; p>0.05). Despite the limitations of this normalization procedure (131,132), it
607	reduces the confounding influence of differences in recording conditions (electrodes placement)
608	and peripheral changes (subcutaneous tissues, muscle mass and architecture) between
609	experimental sessions. In contrast, biceps brachii thickness, as measured by ultrasonography,
610	increased to a greater extent (9.6 vs. 5.5 %; p<0.05) for the 3/7 method. To verify that the brief
611	 C
612	inter-set interval and the incremental number of repetitions in the successive sets in the 3/7 method
613	 C
614	compromised O2 delivery to the active muscles, we compared the changes in tissue oxygenation
615	with near-infrared spectroscopy in biceps brachii and brachioradialis for the 3/7 and 8x6 method
616	A
617	(133). Our data indicated a greater average deficit in oxygenation for the 3/7 method and, in
618	contrast to the 8 x 6 method, an absence of recovery on O2 content between sets.
619	More recently, we compared the 3/7 method to a protocol that reversed the order of the sets (i.e.,
620	7/3 method), similar to a drop-set protocol. Our findings indicated that the gains in 1RM load,
621	 MVC force, and muscle thickness were significantly less (p<0.05) for the 7/3 method compared
622	with the 3/7 method (Figure 2). Although the normalized EMG amplitude of the elbow flexors
623	increased (p<0.05) after both methods, the training gains did not differ significantly.
624	[Figure 2]
625	 D
626	Together, these observations demonstrate that brief inter-set intervals and incremental increases
627	in the number of repetitions performed in successive sets, results in superior outcomes for the 3/7
628	 EP
629	method compared with the 8x6 and 7/3 methods.
630	 TE
631	The greater stimulus for muscle hypertrophy associated with the 3/7 method raises questions
632	about the underlying mechanisms. As observed for low-load exercise training under BFR,
633	shortening the inter-set intervals during high-volume strength training with moderate loads
634	increases the metabolic stress and the acute hormonal response (82,134). Although a short inter-
635	set rest interval (1 min) blunts the rate of myofibrillar protein synthesis in the early post-exercise
636	 C
637	recovery period, but not ~24 h later, compared with longer rest period (5 min) (81), there is no
638	 C
639	clear evidence of an association between an acute increase in myofibrillar protein synthesis after
640	a training session and muscle hypertrophy after a strength training program (135,136). The
641	A
642	suggestion of Schoenfeld and colleagues (17) that inter-sets of ≤ 1 min are likely too brief to
643	promote maximal hypertrophic gains may depend on differences in training variables, such as the
644	total workout relative to the training status of the individual (60,70) and, in particular for trained
645	athletes, the number of sets performed to failure (137,138). With the 3/7 method, the failure
646	stage is reached during the last two sets. The greater gains in 1RM load, MVC force, and muscle
647	 thickness for the 3/7 protocol compared with the 7/3 protocol (same training volume and inter-set
648	rest interval) are consistent with this hypothesis as the 7/3 protocol does not produce task failure.
649	These findings indicate that the effectiveness of the 3/7 method results from a protocol that
650	combines moderate-to-high mechanical tension and metabolic stress (Figure 3). In addition to
651	producing muscle hypertrophy, the 3/7 method also appears to elicit neural adaptions that
652	 D
653	contribute to increases maximal strength. Additional experiments are needed to optimize the
654	training variables (workout volume; optimal rest interval for mono vs. pluri-articular and upper
655	 EP
656	vs. lower body exercises, free weight vs. machine; …) and to determine the relative roles of
657	mechanical tension and metabolic stress in contributing to the outcomes. On a practical point of
658	 TE
659	view, a major advantage of the 3/7 method is its greater efficacy (amount of progress relative to
660	the total number of repetitions) over more classical methods.
661	[Figure 3]
662	 C
663	PERSPECTIVES FOR PROGRESS
664	 C
665	Over the last two decades, our concepts and practice of strength training methods have been
666	strongly shaken. One example is that training with low-load exercise performed until failure or
667	A
668	under BFR may augment muscle protein synthesis (139,140), muscle hypertrophy and maximal
669	strength (25,26,28) to a similar extent as achieved with high-load low volume training in both
670	untrained individuals and trained athletes (for meta-analyses, see 5-8). Another recent change in
671	dogma is that bodybuilding-type training (moderate load, high volume, and brief inter-set
672	interval) is likely not the best strategy to augment muscle protein synthesis and thereby the
673	 increases in muscle growth (see 138). Among many others, these two examples have led to
674	numerous questions at both mechanistic and practical levels.
675	Mechanisms of action
676	A major advance in this field is the observation of an acute increase in muscle protein synthesis
677	within a few hours (4-6 h that remains elevated for more than 24 h) after exercise provided
678	 D
679	nutrition is adequate (see 15,16,135). Unfortunately, the association between the amount of
680	increase in muscle protein synthesis observed in acute condition and its translation into muscle
681	 EP
682	hypertrophy after long-term training remains to be defined (135,136). It is also not clear how
683	successive sessions within a training program, and thus their frequency (number of
684	 TE
685	sessions/week), modulates in fine the amount of muscle growth.
686	One of several possible explanations for the lack of association between muscle hypertrophy and
687	protein synthesis is the way in which muscle CSA is measured. Classically, measures of
688	anatomical CSA or muscle thickness are used to assess the amount of muscle hypertrophy. In
689	 C
690	pennate muscles, however, a more functional measure is the physiological CSA (141), which can
691	 C
692	be accomplished with ultrasonography when the angle of pennation is taken into consideration.
693	Moreover, muscle CSA can be influenced by changes in other factors, such as muscle fiber
694	A
695	swelling in response to training-related damage or modifications in the characteristics of
696	connective tissues (135). Future studies need to assess more carefully the translation of elevated
697	levels of protein synthesis into muscle hypertrophy.
698	 Another issue that needs more attention is the role of anabolic hormones in training-induced
699	adaptations (see 14,50,80,135,136). Many studies have reported a transient increase in the levels
700	of hormones in the blood (testosterone, GH, IGF-1) and their relative concentrations seems to
701	depend of several exercise variables, such as the type of exercise (mono- vs. multi-articular), the
702	workout volume, the inter-set interval (72,118), and whether or not the exercise is performed
703	under BFR (13). Although mechanistic studies suggest that these hormones do not play a direct
704	 D
705	role in muscle protein synthesis (15,16,73), they may have an indirect influence by promoting
706	satellite cell activation and fusion (45,50,80). As exercise-related increases in the levels of these
707	 EP
708	hormones is relatively modest compared with their exogenous administration, it would be useful
709	to determine their dose-dependent effects in both women and men and the influence of various
710	 TE
711	training protocols. The field needs clear experimental designs to establish the functional role, if
712	any, of increases in blood hormone concentrations in acute and long-term adaptations.
713	Although low-load exercise training with BFR is a valid and safe method to increase muscle
714	hypertrophy and strength in frail and sarcopenic patients (see 6,7,12,55), the functional
715	 C
716	consequences for healthy sedentary and older individuals and especially for athletes needs to be
717	 C
718	established. As already mentioned, neural adaptations (i.e., voluntary activation and muscle
719	coordination) play an important role in improving maximal and functional strength (e.g., chair-
720	A
721	rise), but these adaptations are not evident after low-load exercise training with or without BFR.
722	As an example, sedentary and older individuals are typically not able to achieve the maximal
723	level of voluntary activation (142), which reduces their ability to develop maximal strength
724	capacity unless they perform strong contractions on a regular basis (143). Training studies need
725	to distinguish between muscle and neural adaptations to identify the relative training-related
726	 responses to low-load and high-load exercises. Approaches are to use electrophysiological
727	methods, such as the superimposed twitch technique, to quantify activation-related adaptations
728	(144) or more insightful methods (see 18) to obtain information on adaptive mechanisms.
729	In addition to maximal strength, the development of explosive strength (rate of force
730	development/power) is necessary for many athletes and for older persons so that they produce a
731	 D
732	reactive response as quickly as possible when balance is compromised (145). Training with rapid
733	contractions increases both the level of voluntary activation (146) and muscle-tendon stiffness
734	 EP
735	(147). Increases in muscle-tendon stiffness, which improve the rate at which force is transmitted
736	to the skeleton (148), can be improved by employing high-load concentric or eccentric
737	 TE
738	contractions (149,150) and stretch-shortening-type contractions (151,152). As exercise training
739	under BFR involves low loads and is performed slowly, there are currently no clear evidences
740	that this training modality is effective to increase muscle-tendon stiffness substantially (35,153).
741	Practical aspects
742	 C
743	In absence of a clear association between muscle hypertrophy and the levels of metabolic stress
744	 C
745	as the consequence of the ischemic/hypoxic environment (11,154), Pearson and Hussain (13)
746	suggested that the influence of mechanical tension and metabolic stress may be additive (Figure
747	A
748	3). However, the relative contributions of these primary factors are not known. Also, the gains
749	achieved by combining high-load and low-load exercises with BFR in the same session or in
750	separate sessions need to be compared with a program of moderate-load strength training with
751	brief inter-set intervals (such as the 3/7 method). Well-designed studies are needed to investigate
752	whether it is more effective to optimize the effects of mechanical tension and metabolic stress by
753	 combining low-load exercise with BFR and high-load strength training or to use a protocol with
754	moderate loads and brief inter-set intervals to induce a high level of metabolic stress. An
755	alternative approach, as used by competitive athletes for many years, is to periodize (block
756	training) complementary methods throughout a long-term training program (2). Here also,
757	investigations are needed to determine the most appropriate protocol or the best combination of
758	protocols.
759	 D
760	An additional practical criterion that needs to be considered for persons who have time
761	 EP
762	constraints, is the benefit to cost ratio (amount of progress relative to the time spent during
763	training) of the different protocols. This is also critical for well-trained athlete to improve the
764	 TE
765	efficacy of their training programs and to limit the risk of overtraining. In this context, the 3/7
766	protocol is appealing as one bout of a given exercise can be completed in ~1.5 min.
767	In conclusion, recent studies reporting contradictory findings to our well-established knowledge
768	have challenged contemporary concepts about strength training. This uncertainty should be used
769	 C
770	as an opportunity to advance the field by augmenting our knowledge on the adaptive
771	 C
772	neuromuscular mechanisms of strength and power training, and by offering more consistent
773	guidelines. As the neuromuscular adaptations are modulated by numerous criteria (e.g., age, sex,
774	A
775	individual training status and experience, workout volume, number of sessions per week, and
776	muscle group), much remains to be done to determine the optimal training dose that maximizes
777	the performance gains achieved by persons with varying characteristics.

 ABSTRACT
Training with low-load exercise performed under blood-flow restriction can augment muscle
hypertrophy and maximal strength to a similar extent as the classical high-load strength training
method. However, the blood-flow restriction method elicits only minor neural adaptations. In an
attempt to maximize training-related gains, we propose using other protocols that combine high
voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
 D
 EP
SUMMARY for Table of Contents: In an attempt to maximize training-related gains in
 TE
maximal strength and muscle hypertrophy, we propose to design new protocols that combine
high mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
KEY WORDS: Mechanical tension; metabolic stress; blood flow restriction; muscle
 C
hypertrophy; neural adaptations
 C
A
 KEY POINTS
 Mechanical tension and metabolic stress contribute to training-related muscle hypertrophy
 and increases in maximal strength.
 As the magnitude of the neural adaptations after low-load exercise with blood flow
 restriction are less than those elicited by high-load strength training and this method is
 difficult for some individuals and insufficient for well-trained athletes, we suggest there is a

 need for new strength-training protocols.
 D
 One training option is to combine different levels of mechanical tension and metabolic stress
 EP
 that are optimized to the training status of the individual.
 TE
 C
 C
A
 INTRODUCTION
The increase in muscle strength is classically based on the "overload" principle (1). This
principle, which states that a minimal load/contraction intensity must be exceeded during the
training sessions to increase muscle strength, is used in sport training and in clinical and
rehabilitation settings. Based on this concept, moderate-to-high mechanical loading of the
muscle (≥60-70% of the one repetition maximum - 1RM) has long been considered as the main
 D
stimulus (i.e., mechanical tension) for muscle hypertrophy and thereby an increase in muscle
strength (2-4). More recently, however, studies using training loads of less than 50% of 1RM
 EP
performed until failure (5) or with blood-flow restriction (BFR) (ischemic/hypoxic condition)
have reported gains in maximal strength and comparable levels of muscle hypertrophy to that
 TE
observed with conventional heavy-load strength training (for recent reviews, see 6-8). These
studies suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites (i.e., metabolic stress) may
play a role in the exercise stimulus leading to an increased accretion of muscle mass and strength
(9-10).
 C
The current Perspective for Progress paper compares training programs performed with high
 C
loads to those involving low loads under BFR and the adaptations elicited by each approach. As
one of the objectives was to examine the possible contribution of metabolic stress on muscle
A
hypertrophy, we chosen to compare low-load exercise with BFR to high-load strength training,
as the former method produce more metabolic stress and needs fewer repetitions to reach failure
(i.e. greater efficacy) than low-load training performed under normal blood circulation (5). We
also explore the utility of the approach of combining moderate-to-high loads (mechanical stress)
and brief rest intervals between sets (metabolic stress) to maximize muscle hypertrophy and
 strength gains in untrained and trained individuals. Although the efficacy of low-load training
with BFR is particularly relevant for patients and healthy untrained or aged individuals, for
whom heavy-load strength training may be problematic and contra-indicated (6-8,11,12), such
training may be insufficient in well-trained athletes who require high level of strength or power
(13).
 D
Although increases in maximal strength are due to both muscle and neural adaptations, the
purpose of our article is not to provide an in-depth review of the molecular mechanisms
 EP
underlying muscle hypertrophy, nor to discuss the numerous neural adaptations induced by
strength training. Such information can be found in the following reviews on muscle (13-17) and
 TE
neural (18-22) adaptations.
HIGH-LOAD STRENGTH TRAINING VS. LOW-LOAD EXERCISE WITH BFR
Muscle adaptations to high-load strength training
Based on a substantial literature on traditional strength training, the American College of Sport
 C
Medicine (2) recommends the use of moderate loads (70-85% of 1RM, 8-12 repetition per set for
 C
1-3 sets per exercise) for novice and intermediate individuals and high loads (70-100% of 1RM,
1-12 repetitions per set for a minimum of 3-6 sets per exercise) for trained athletes to increase
A
both muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength.
High mechanical loading of the muscle (≥70% of 1RM) is traditionally considered to be an
essential stimulus for increases in maximal strength (2-5,21,23). At the muscle level, the primary
adaptation is an increase in muscle size (i.e., hypertrophy). Strength training increases force
 capacity by increasing the quantity of contractile proteins in individual muscle fibers and thereby
the cross-sectional area of muscle. In pennate muscles (e.g., gastrocnenmii, vastus medialis and
lateralis), however, the angle of pennation of muscle fascicles increases with strength training
(24,25), which reduces the force contributed by each fiber to the tendon (longitudinal force
vector) due to an increase in the oblique angle of pull. The training-related increase in the force
produced by individual muscle fibers in pennate muscles, therefore, is attenuated by increases in
 D
the pennation angle (22,24). The magnitude of this adaptation likely explains some of the
variability between muscle strength and anatomical cross-sectional area seen among individuals.
 EP
Although it has been instructed for a long time that muscle hypertrophy is greater when the
 TE
exercise involves a moderate load (~70% of 1RM) with many repetitions than a higher load
(>80% 1RM) with fewer repetitions (2,26,27), more recent publications do not support that
claim, at least in untrained or medium-trained individuals (see 5). The meta-analysis by
Schoenfeld and colleagues (5) even indicates that similar gains in muscle hypertrophy can be
obtained for a large range of loads (~30–80% of maximum) provided that sets are performed to
 C
failure. A load equal to 20% of 1RM appears, however, insufficient to promote muscle
 C
hypertrophy (28). In contrast, greater gains in maximal strength are observed for training with
higher load (> 60% of 1RM) compared with lower load (≤ 60% of 1RM). The relative greater
A
increase in maximal strength than in muscle hypertrophy with high-load training is usually
explained primarily by a greater contribution of neural changes (2,18,21) and muscle cytoskeletal
remodelling associated with force transmission (29).
 Muscle adaptations to low-load exercise under BFR
In the mid-1990s, it was suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites may
contribute to an increased accretion of muscle mass and maximal strength (9,10). This idea was
supported by subsequent studies showing that training with loads ranging from 20 to 50% of
1RM performed under BFR increased muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength (30,31). In
these studies, blood flow was restricted to a muscle group by the application of external pressure
 D
via a tourniquet, an inflated cuff, or an elastic band applied over the proximal portion of either
the upper or lower extremities. This external pressure varied across muscle groups and studies,
 EP
but typically ranged from 60 to 270 mmHg (7). In most conditions, the external pressure applied
around the limb was sufficient to maintain some arterial flow, but blocked venous blood return
 TE
distal to the occlusion site (32). Such reduction in blood flow induces an ischemic/hypoxic
environment that may augment the training effect of the exercised muscle compared with the
normal blood-flow condition (30,31).
The gains in muscle size and strength achieved with low-load exercise training performed under
 C
BFR have been reported to be similar to those elicited by conventional heavy-load strength
 C
training. For example, Takarada and colleagues (31) reported that a 16-week (2 sessions/week)
low-load (50% of 1RM) exercise training of the elbow flexor muscles performed under BFR
A
(100 mmHg) increased muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and strength (~19% and 18%,
respectively), which was similar to the increases (~15% and 22.5%) achieved with high-intensity
strength training (80% of 1RM) without BFR and much more than an identical low-intensity
(50% of 1RM) protocol without ischemia (~5% and 1%). Similar observations have been
reported with lower loads combined with BFR (20-30% of 1RM; 33-35). Even in athletes, low-
 load (20% of 1RM) training with the knee extensors performed under hypoxic or vascular-
occlusion conditions led to similar increases in maximal strength (14.8 vs. 13.3 %) and muscle
hypertrophy (6.1 vs. 6.6%) (36). This exercise stimulus, however, may be insufficient to increase
the 1RM load in well-trained athletes (37) as, for example, powerlifters (38).
Meta-analyses comparison
 D
Depending of the inclusion criteria adopted, recent meta-analyses have reached slightly different
conclusions (6-8). One analysis on patients suffering from musculoskeletal disease (7) and
 EP
another analysis on various population of individuals (8) both indicated that the increase in
muscle strength was less after low-load exercise training with BFR than with high-load strength
 TE
training. In the latter meta-analysis (8), between-group comparisons indicated significantly
greater gains (~7%) in muscle strength for high-load strength training than for low-load exercise
training with BFR. Similar findings were observed when the gain in muscle strength was
evaluated with the same exercise modality used during training (1RM with an inertial load,
isometric contraction, or isokinetic testing). However, none of the characteristics related to the
 C
level of external blood pressure, cuff width, or external pressure prescription (individualized or
 C
not) appears to have influenced the gain in muscle strength.
A
In contrast, the meta-analysis performed by Gronfeldt and colleagues (6), which included results
on healthy populations ranging from young to older adults and from untrained to well-trained
participants, found no differences between the two training methods. This conclusion is likely a
consequence of the more restrictive inclusion criteria. For example, studies that used within-
subject measurements (e.g., comparison of muscles from ipsi- and contralateral limb) or subjects
 not randomized were not included in the meta-analysis. In addition, only one strength variable
was extracted in studies that obtained multiple strength outcomes (1RM load and isometric MVC
or isokinetic testing) in the same subjects. Also, the inclusion criteria did not distinguish between
studies performed on individuals with different training histories (patients, sedentary, or trained)
or account for differences in sex or age.
 D
The capacity of training with low loads under BFR to increase muscle mass was reviewed in the
meta-analysis by Lixandrao and colleagues (8). The results indicated similar levels of muscle
 EP
hypertrophy (average gain difference of <1% in favor of high-load strength training) with the
two methods. As noted for the increases in maximal strength, blood pressure-related parameters
 TE
do not seem to influence the level of muscle hypertrophy.
Overall, these meta-analyses suggest that low-load exercise training with BFR is an effective
method to increase maximal strength; the effect is greater than that achieved with a similar
training load without BFR when the number of repetitions is equated (7). Nonetheless, its
 C
relative efficacy compared with conventional high-load strength training seems to depend on the
 C
comparison group (see above). As low-load training with BFR is relatively safe (7,11,12), it can
be an alternative to high-load strength training as a method to increase neuromuscular capacities
A
in patients (7) and healthy sedentary or active young and older adults (6,8), but is likely an
insufficient stimulus for well-trained athletes (37,38). However, the mechanisms by which the
metabolic stress elicited by BFR contribute to muscle hypertrophy and strength gains is currently
unclear.
 MECHANISMS CONTRIBUTING TO MUSCLE HYPERTROPHY
Mechanical factors
Early animal studies found that mechanical tension acts as a primary mechanism for muscle
growth and thereby increases in muscle strength (for a review, see 39). For example, removal of
a synergist muscle (i.e., chronic overload) led to the hypertrophy of the remaining muscles (40)
and increases in the mechanical strain on a muscle attenuated the atrophy caused by unloading
 D
(41). Subsequent, studies found that imposing high mechanical tension and/or lengthening of
activated muscles is a major mediator of myofibril protein synthesis (42).
 EP
Mechanotransduction and growth factors
 TE
Muscle hypertrophy observed after chronic mechanical overload results from an increase in the
net protein synthesis and in the number of myonuclei that mediate the increase in the volume of
contractile proteins within a muscle fiber (15). The process by which the mechanical stress is
translated into chemical signals that trigger an intracellular signaling cascade leading ultimately
to the production of muscle proteins is known as mechanotransduction. Briefly, in presence of
 C
chronic muscle overload, focal adhesion kinases (FAK) bind to mechanoreceptors (i.e., integrin
 C
receptors) that connect the extracellular matrix to the sarcolemma. Through its action, FAK
converts mechanical tension into a chemical signal that mediates intracellular anabolic
A
(mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 - mTORC1) and catabolic (family of transcription
factors - FOXO) pathways (for more details, see 15,16,43). When associated with sufficient
nutritional intake (15, 44), this process favors protein synthesis over its degradation, resulting in
a net increase in contractile protein and muscle-fiber hypertrophy (Figure 1; 16).
 [Figure 1]
The mTORC1 is not solely activated by high mechanical loads, but also other stimuli such as
insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and one of its variants termed mechanogrowth factor
(MGF). MGF is produced locally and contributes to up-regulate protein synthesis via the
activation of the P13K/Akt /mTORC1 pathway (for reviews see 15,16,43,45). Due of its rapid
 D
expression following mechanical loading, MGF contributes to enhance the post-exercise
hypertrophic response and to facilitate local repair of muscle damage (Figure 1; 46), but its
 EP
intervention does not seem to be obligatory for muscle growth (15,47).
Satellite cells
 TE
In addition to mechanotransduction and growth factors, new nuclei are differentiated from
“satellite cells” that are quiescent mononucleated cells located under the basal lamina (48).
Although muscle damage associated with strength training exercises, and in particular with
lengthening/eccentric contractions, elicits satellite cells activation and proliferation (49), the
 C
actual stimulus needed to activate satellite cells is not known. Pathways involving intracellular
 C
signalling via mechano-sensitive receptors or indirectly through growth factor-mediated signals
and hormonal release (50,51) are the most likely candidates (Figure 1; Kadi et al., 2005; Hanssen
A
et al., 2013). When activated, satellite cells begin proliferating and some of them fuse with
muscle fiber to add new nuclei to the existing fibers (48,52,53). These new myonuclei produce
mRNA and contribute to the production of contractile proteins in response to both high-load
strength training (48,53) and low-load exercise with BFR (54). It seems, however, that some
 muscle hypertrophy can occur without the addition of myonuclei to existing fibers, but their
inclusion is necessary for larger increases (>25%) in muscle size (52)
Although most experimental evidence suggests that the hypertrophy of the individual muscle
fibers is the main mechanism for the increase in muscle mass, hyperplasia (i.e., increase in the
number of muscle fibers) may contribute to an increase in muscle size. However, the extent to
 D
which hyperplasia can occur in humans who participate in long-term strength training (e.g.,
bodybuilders) appears relatively weak (55) or nonexistent (4). Based on immunohistochemical
 EP
techniques, Kadi and colleagues (48,56) proposed that in addition to their role in the hypertrophy
of the existing muscle fibers, satellite cells may fuse to develop new muscles fibers. For example,
 TE
Kadi and Thornell (56) showed that elite powerlifters, contrary to untrained subjects, displayed
small-diameter fibers that expressed embryonic and neonatal myosin heavy-chain (MHC)
isoforms, which are considered to be markers for the early stages of muscle fiber development.
Despite these observations, the role of hyperplasia appears rather weak in humans and fiber
hypertrophy is the primary mechanism responsible for increases in muscle mass after strength
training. C
 C
Metabolic factors
A
Given the low mechanical stress that occurs during BFR, it has been suggested that muscle
hypertrophy under this condition may not be due to mechanotransduction and the IGF-
1/P13K/Akt /mTORC1 pathway (13,57,58), and other mechanisms have been proposed (Figure
1; for reviews, see 11,13,57). Among the possible mechanisms, we have chosen to evoke the
potential direct effects of an increase in the level of metabolites and on systemic hormones and
 muscle activation (Figure 1; 13,58). Other secondary mechanisms, including notably cell
swelling, muscle damage, and increased production of reactive oxygen species have been
proposed to play an indirect role in muscle hypertrophy (see 13,57).
The hypoxic/ischemic condition produced by low-load occlusion training reduces O2 supply to
the involved muscles and induces a shift from aerobic towards anaerobic metabolism, which has
 D
consequences for the rate of ATP rephosphorylation. Low levels of O2 further accentuates the
alterations in ionic concentration gradients (K+, Na+, Ca2+, …) and the accumulation of
 EP
metabolic by-products, including lactate, hydrogen ions (H+), inorganic phosphate (Pi), ADP, …
(59). Such metabolic stress may act as an anabolic signal (60-62) that engages the mitogen-
 TE
activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Figure 1; 57,63). The MAPK pathway does not
depend on the exercise load and may be regulated by a metabolic sensor (64).
Although an association between Pi or intramuscular pH and muscle hypertrophy has been
observed after low-intensity (20% of 1RM) exercise training with BFR (65), there seems to be a
 C
potential role for lactate in muscle hypertrophy (61). For example, blood lactate concentration is
 C
significantly greater after training with low-load exercise under BFR (31) and environmental
hypoxia (36,66) than for the same exercise protocol performed under normal conditions.
A
Furthermore, greater relative blood lactate concentration, as occurs after low-load exercise with
BFR, is accompanied by a greater increase in muscle CSA after the training program compared
with high-load or low-load exercise performed in normal conditions (31). These in vivo
observations are supported by in vitro studies showing the anabolic properties of lactate. In cell
culture preparations, lactate induces myogenesis (67,68) and increase phosphorylation of
 p70S6K (a down-stream target of mTORC1) (67). Moreover, a rodent model further indicated
that high concentrations of lactate appear to modulate muscle differentiation by regulating the
associated networks of myogenic protein determination, enhancing MHC expression and
myotube hypertrophy (69).
Hormonal modulation
 D
For a number of years it has been suggested that muscle hypertrophy in response to a strength
training was due, at least in part, to a transient increase (~30 min) in systemic anabolic hormones
 EP
(testosterone, GH, IGF-1) after a training session in both untrained individuals and trained
athletes (14,70-73).
 TE
The proponents of a role for testosterone in muscle hypertrophy suggest either a direct effect by
its binding on androgen receptors that mediate gene transcription (71,72,74) or an indirect effect
that includes potentiating the release of other anabolic hormones such as growth hormone (GH)
and IGF-1/MGF (75,76), or mediating satellite cell activation and proliferation (Figure 1; 50,51).
 C
Despite the recognized role of testosterone in developmental processes that regulate muscle
 C
growth and hypertrophy after administration of supra-physiological dose of testosterone (77), the
augmentation of serum concentrations after strength training may be insufficient to trigger
A
muscle hypertrophy (15,16). As a causal link between acute testosterone production and
hypertrophy has not been established and post-exercise increases in testosterone are not required
for muscle hypertrophy (see 73,78,79), further studies are needed to determine its functional role,
if any, in training-related muscle adaptations (80).
 The influence of GH and IGF-1 on the development of muscle mass after strength training is also
unclear as its direct involvement in muscle hypertrophy appears negligible (73,81). Nonetheless,
others have found that the effects of GH and circulating IGF-1 might be complementary in
maximizing muscle anabolism, thereby optimizing the adaptations (45,80). For example, GH
might increase the net muscle protein synthesis indirectly by facilitating amino acid transport and
availability via both endocrine and locally produced IGF-1/MGF (82) or by inducing muscle
 D
growth through satellite cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation (Figure 1; see 15,45,50).
As GH can enhance collagen protein synthesis (83), it has been suggested that such adaptations
 EP
could, through improved force transmission (29), enable the use of higher loads during training,
which in turn might stimulate muscle protein synthesis (16). However, several studies have
 TE
reported that a single session of low-intensity exercise performed under BFR increases the level
of GH in the blood drastically (84-86) and to a greater extent than when the same exercise is
performed to failure with normal blood circulation or blood flow occlusion without exercise (84).
In addition, serum GH increases to a much greater extent in response to low-load exercise under
BFR than for higher-load (70% of 1RM) exercise performed under normal conditions (85).
 C
Despite the enhanced blood GH concentration in both traditional strength-training program and
 C
ischemic/hypoxic conditions, it is currently not clear how such increases can contribute to the
adaptations that underlie muscle hypertrophy.
A
Muscle activation
Another often suggested explanation for the efficacy of low-load exercise training performed
under BFR is via the indirect action of metabolites on augmenting muscle activation (58,79,87).
When exercises are performed with submaximal loads in unrestricted blood-flow conditions, an
 increase in synaptic input to the motor neuron pool is needed to recruit progressively higher-
threshold motor units to compensate for fatigue-related decrease in force of the activated motor
units when the task progress towards failure (88). Although fatigue-related declines in force
capacity are multifactorial and cannot solely be attributed to the accumulation of metabolites (see
89), Pi, H+, and others are known to impair intramuscular mechanisms associated with force
production (90,91). When blood flow is occluded, this effect is further amplified by the lack of
O2 (92).
 D
 EP
In normal blood-flow conditions, complete recruitment of motor units in limb muscles is reached
when the muscle is contracting at high force levels. However, as low-threshold motor units are
 TE
sensitive to an O2 deficit (93), as it occurs during contractions with BFR, recruitment range is
likely compressed and higher-threshold motor units are recruited at lower forces. Due to this
effect, it is often assumed that most motor units are recruited at task failure during low-load
ischemic exercises (13,15,31,58). This assumption is indirectly supported by studies showing
that BFR conditions augment surface EMG amplitude to a greater extent than in unrestricted
 C
blood-flow condition during load- and volume-matched protocols (94,95) but to a similar EMG
 C
amplitude when both protocols are performed to failure (96).
A
However, it is noteworthy that low-load (15-20%) exercise that is either sustained (97,98) or
intermittent (99) until task failure in a no-cuff condition does not reach the maximal EMG
amplitude recorded before the fatigue protocol. In contrast, repeated movements with a load
equal or superior to 40% of 1RM reached near-maximal or maximal EMG at task failure (99).
Despite the limitations (signal cancellation) of surface EMG recording to infer the level of neural
 drive sent to the muscle during fatiguing contractions (100), it is unlikely that the entire pool of
motor units is maximally activated (recruitment and discharge rate) at the completion of each set
of exercises even in BFR conditions.
The metabolic and ionic changes in the muscle during fatiguing contractions activate small-
diameter afferents of group III & IV fibers (101) that induce progressive inhibitory effects at
 D
both spinal and supraspinal levels, further limiting muscle activation (102) and interrupting the
activity of some motor units (88). As blood flow occlusion augments the production of metabolic
 EP
by-products, the inhibitory effect of group III & IV fibers is likely intensified (103,104).
Although glycogen depletion has been reported in type II fibers following low-load exercise
 TE
(30% of 1RM) performed in unrestricted blood flow condition until task failure (105), this
observation does not mean that the corresponding motor units discharged at rates high enough to
develop their maximal force capacity. Therefore, the hypothesis that low-load exercise
performed under BFR activates all motor units as in high-load exercise and elicits sufficient
mechanical tension to trigger protein synthesis (13,31,58) is not convincing and needs to be more
 C
carefully examined.
 C
Collectively, these findings indicate that even though increases in muscle strength after a
A
traditional strength-training program is due to an increase in muscle mass (24,106), the
mechanisms that produce muscle hypertrophy either through the mechanotransduction pathway
or indirectly via growth factors-mediated signals still remain a matter of debate (15,16,52,57,58).
Furthermore, despite the experimental evidences that low-load exercise performed under BFR
 can produce similar gains in muscle performance as high-load strength training, potential
alternative mechanisms to the mechanotransduction pathway remain to be defined.
CONTRIBUTION OF NEURAL ADAPTATIONS TO MAXIMAL STRENGTH
It has been known for many years that strength gains elicited by high-load strength training
involve both neural and muscular adaptations (107). Indirect evidence of neural adaptations
 D
includes the dissociation between the magnitude of structural (muscle size) and functional
changes (108). Several methods have been used to measure changes in muscle activation during
 EP
maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) after completing a strength-training program: surface
EMG activity (107,109), superimposed electrical stimulation method (110,111), ratio of evoked
 TE
tetanic force to MVC force (112), and maximal discharge rates of motor units (113). Despite
some technical limitations with these approaches (see 20), these studies reported an increase in
the level of voluntary activation (i.e., degree of motor unit recruitment and discharge rate) after
strength training that may account for ~1/3 of the increase in maximal strength (114). More
insightful electrophysiological approaches (see 18) have further indicated that neural adaptations
 C
are located at both supraspinal and spinal levels (see 19,114).
 C
Among the few studies that have investigated the neural adaptations in response to low-load
A
exercise training under BFR, the conclusions appear contrasting. One study reported an increase
in surface EMG amplitude of the two vastii during an MVC with the knee extensors after a 5-
week training program with a load of 20% of 1RM (115). In contrast, other studies have not
found any changes in surface EMG amplitude after 8-12 weeks of training with a load of 20 or
50% of 1RM under BFR for the knee extensors (35) or elbow flexors (116), respectively. In
 addition, studies using electrophysiological approaches have not observed any changes in the
level of voluntary activation as tested with the superimposed twitch technique (35,116) or
assessing the descending drive (V-wave response) and responsiveness of a spinal reflex pathway
(H-reflex) (117). These studies indicate that low-load exercise training under BFR induces no
more than minor neural adaptations compared with those classically found after high-load
strength training (18,20-22).
 D
Together, these findings suggest that although low-load exercise training under BFR can be
 EP
effective in increasing muscle mass and maximal strength, it does not appear to modulate all
strength- and power-related parameters, particularly those associated with voluntary muscle
activation.

HOW TO MAXIMIZE NEUROMUSCULAR ADAPTATIONS?
Influence of inter-set interval
As suggested by Pearson & Hussain (13), one strategy to maximize strength gains is to use
 C
training protocols that combine high levels of both mechanical tension and metabolic stress. This
 C
can be achieved by alternating high-load and low-load exercise under BFR either in the same or
separate training sessions. Alternatively, this goal could be accomplished by using moderate-to-
A
high loads (high mechanical tension) with brief inter-set rest intervals to generate high metabolic
stress in a brief period of time.
In addition to major training variables, such as the load intensity and training volume (2,17,118),
the rest interval between sets influences the outcomes produced by a strength-training program.
 The classical recommendations for inter-set intervals are based on the training goal (maximal
strength, muscle hypertrophy, muscle power, muscular endurance) and the ability to maintain the
number of repetitions within a prescribed zone over consecutive sets (2,118). For example,
specific training protocols differ between bodybuilders and powerlifters/weightlifters. Although
both types of athletes train with high-to-very high loads, powerlifters typically use few (1- 8)
repetitions in each set and long inter-set intervals (>2-3 min), whereas bodybuilders use more
 D
repetitions (8-10) in each set performed until failure and shorter rest periods (≤ 1 min)
(26,27,119). Practical wisdom suggests that the bodybuilding protocol favors muscle
 EP
hypertrophy, whereas the powerlifting protocol leads to greater muscle strength (27).
Nonetheless, there is no consensus on the specificity of these adaptations (see below and review
papers by 17,118,120).
 TE
One well-accepted notion is that reducing the recovery period between sets (from 5-3 min to1
min) decreases the total number of repetitions with a constant load that can be completed in a
multiple sets training, which impacts the total training volume (2,118,121). In addition, more
 C
than 3 min of rest may be needed to maintain maximal strength and power during successive sets
 C
and to accumulate a high training volume, depending of the training status of the individual, the
muscle group being targeted, and the type of exercise (single vs. multi-joint exercise) performed
A
(17,118). A 3-min interval allows enough time for the resynthesis of phosphocreatine (PCr)
through the aerobic system (59) and the elimination of part of intracellular metabolic by-products
into the blood stream. When associated with limited O2 availability (i.e., hypoxia), these
alterations slow down the rate of PCr resynthesis and ADP rephosphorylation, which reduce both
the maximal strength and speed of contraction (59).
 Several studies have shown that rest intervals of 2-3 min result in significantly greater increases
in maximal strength and power compared with shorter rest intervals (30-90 s) (17,120,122-124).
Although necessary to maximize the level of voluntary activation and thereby maximal strength,
the maintenance of training intensity during successive sets is not usually chosen when
attempting to induce muscle hypertrophy (27). The experimental evidence on the influence of
 D
short (≤ 1 min) and long (≥ 3 min) inter-set intervals during strength training is mixed. Some
studies showed an advantage of long inter-set intervals for muscle hypertrophy (74,125), whereas
 EP
others found either better result with short inter-set intervals (126) or no significant difference
(127,128).
 TE
Unfortunately, the workout volume in the two training programs was not matched in all these
studies (74,128) which likely influenced the conclusion. In contrast, Goto and colleagues (60)
compared the outcomes achieved with a 12-week strength training program for two groups of
subjects who performed protocols that were matched for volume and load intensity (3-5 sets of
 C
10 reps at 70-75% of 1RM with an inter-set rest period of 1 min). One group performed the
 C
repetitions in each set without any interruption, whereas the other group had a 30-s rest period
after the first 5 repetitions of each set. As expected, blood lactate concentration was significantly
A
greater for the protocol that did not include the 30-s rest. The main finding was that muscle CSA
only increased significantly in the group that did not include a rest period during each set
indicating that a strength training protocol leading to high accumulation of metabolic by-product
may favour muscle hypertrophy.
 In search of new training strategies
Recent work from our laboratory has examined the effectiveness of a new training design (called
the 3/7 method) to promote strength gains in the bench press exercise performed by physically
active individuals (129). This method, based on a strength training protocol introduced by a
French coach named Emmanuel Légeard, is characterized by 5 sets of an incremental number of
repetitions per set (from 3 repetitions in the first set to 7 repetitions in the last set) with a constant
 D
load of ~70% of 1RM. Each set was separated by a very brief rest interval of 15 s. When
compared with the more "classical" method of a constant number of repetitions in each set and
 EP
matching the load and number of repetitions (i.e., training volume; 4x6 method: 4 sets of 6
repetitions with 150-s rest interval between sets), the 3/7 method produced a significantly
 TE
(p<0.05) greater increase in 1 RM load (29.8 vs. 21.8% for the 4x6 method) and maximal
strength (22.4 vs. 9.9% for the 4x6 method) as tested with an isokinetic device (Ariel
Computerized Exercise System, Ariel Dynamic Inc.) after 12 weeks (2 sessions/week) of training
(129). Doubling the number of sets performed with the classical method (i.e., 8 sets of 6
repetitions) slightly increased (p<0.05) the gain in 1RM load (35.9%) compared with the 3/7
 C
method, but the increase in maximal strength did not differ (p>0.05) between the two protocols
 C
(25.5 vs. 22.4%). Also, the increase in peak power was greater (p<0.05) for the 8x6 (21.6%)
compared with the 3/7 (16.3%) method, but the difference was not significant (p>0.05) when
A
volume was matched for the two protocols (i.e., 3/7 vs. 4x6) (129).
Subsequently, we examined the relative contributions of neural and muscular adaptations to the

protocol was repeated twice with a 150-s rest between the two bouts and compared with the 8x6
method; 150 s of rest between sets. Our results indicated that both protocols (3/7 and 8x6)

MVC force (p=0.07) for the 3/7 method.

The EMG activity of two elbow flexors (long head of biceps brachii and brachioradialis),

normalized to their respective maximal M wave (Mmax) elicited by supramaximal electrical

(14.5 vs. 8.1%; p>0.05). Despite the limitations of this normalization procedure (131,132), it

and peripheral changes (subcutaneous tissues, muscle mass and architecture) between

 C
inter-set interval and the incremental number of repetitions in the successive sets in the 3/7 method

A
(133). Our data indicated a greater average deficit in oxygenation for the 3/7 method and, in

Together, these observations demonstrate that brief inter-set intervals and incremental increases

method compared with the 8x6 and 7/3 methods.

The greater stimulus for muscle hypertrophy associated with the 3/7 method raises questions

clear evidence of an association between an acute increase in myofibrillar protein synthesis after

A

contribute to increases maximal strength. Additional experiments are needed to optimize the

 EP
vs. lower body exercises, free weight vs. machine; …) and to determine the relative roles of

view, a major advantage of the 3/7 method is its greater efficacy (amount of progress relative to

PERSPECTIVES FOR PROGRESS
 C
Over the last two decades, our concepts and practice of strength training methods have been
strongly shaken. One example is that training with low-load exercise performed until failure or
A
under BFR may augment muscle protein synthesis (139,140), muscle hypertrophy and maximal
strength (25,26,28) to a similar extent as achieved with high-load low volume training in both
untrained individuals and trained athletes (for meta-analyses, see 5-8). Another recent change in
dogma is that bodybuilding-type training (moderate load, high volume, and brief inter-set
interval) is likely not the best strategy to augment muscle protein synthesis and thereby the
 increases in muscle growth (see 138). Among many others, these two examples have led to
numerous questions at both mechanistic and practical levels.
Mechanisms of action
A major advance in this field is the observation of an acute increase in muscle protein synthesis
within a few hours (4-6 h that remains elevated for more than 24 h) after exercise provided
 D
nutrition is adequate (see 15,16,135). Unfortunately, the association between the amount of
increase in muscle protein synthesis observed in acute condition and its translation into muscle
 EP
hypertrophy after long-term training remains to be defined (135,136). It is also not clear how
successive sessions within a training program, and thus their frequency (number of
 TE
sessions/week), modulates in fine the amount of muscle growth.
One of several possible explanations for the lack of association between muscle hypertrophy and
protein synthesis is the way in which muscle CSA is measured. Classically, measures of
anatomical CSA or muscle thickness are used to assess the amount of muscle hypertrophy. In
 C
pennate muscles, however, a more functional measure is the physiological CSA (141), which can
 C
be accomplished with ultrasonography when the angle of pennation is taken into consideration.
Moreover, muscle CSA can be influenced by changes in other factors, such as muscle fiber
A
swelling in response to training-related damage or modifications in the characteristics of
connective tissues (135). Future studies need to assess more carefully the translation of elevated
levels of protein synthesis into muscle hypertrophy.
 Another issue that needs more attention is the role of anabolic hormones in training-induced
adaptations (see 14,50,80,135,136). Many studies have reported a transient increase in the levels
of hormones in the blood (testosterone, GH, IGF-1) and their relative concentrations seems to
depend of several exercise variables, such as the type of exercise (mono- vs. multi-articular), the
workout volume, the inter-set interval (72,118), and whether or not the exercise is performed
under BFR (13). Although mechanistic studies suggest that these hormones do not play a direct
 D
role in muscle protein synthesis (15,16,73), they may have an indirect influence by promoting
satellite cell activation and fusion (45,50,80). As exercise-related increases in the levels of these
 EP
hormones is relatively modest compared with their exogenous administration, it would be useful
to determine their dose-dependent effects in both women and men and the influence of various
 TE
training protocols. The field needs clear experimental designs to establish the functional role, if
any, of increases in blood hormone concentrations in acute and long-term adaptations.
Although low-load exercise training with BFR is a valid and safe method to increase muscle
hypertrophy and strength in frail and sarcopenic patients (see 6,7,12,55), the functional
 C
consequences for healthy sedentary and older individuals and especially for athletes needs to be
 C
established. As already mentioned, neural adaptations (i.e., voluntary activation and muscle
coordination) play an important role in improving maximal and functional strength (e.g., chair-
A
rise), but these adaptations are not evident after low-load exercise training with or without BFR.
As an example, sedentary and older individuals are typically not able to achieve the maximal
level of voluntary activation (142), which reduces their ability to develop maximal strength
capacity unless they perform strong contractions on a regular basis (143). Training studies need
to distinguish between muscle and neural adaptations to identify the relative training-related
 responses to low-load and high-load exercises. Approaches are to use electrophysiological
methods, such as the superimposed twitch technique, to quantify activation-related adaptations
(144) or more insightful methods (see 18) to obtain information on adaptive mechanisms.
In addition to maximal strength, the development of explosive strength (rate of force
development/power) is necessary for many athletes and for older persons so that they produce a
 D
reactive response as quickly as possible when balance is compromised (145). Training with rapid
contractions increases both the level of voluntary activation (146) and muscle-tendon stiffness
 EP
(147). Increases in muscle-tendon stiffness, which improve the rate at which force is transmitted
to the skeleton (148), can be improved by employing high-load concentric or eccentric
 TE
contractions (149,150) and stretch-shortening-type contractions (151,152). As exercise training
under BFR involves low loads and is performed slowly, there are currently no clear evidences
that this training modality is effective to increase muscle-tendon stiffness substantially (35,153).
Practical aspects
 C
In absence of a clear association between muscle hypertrophy and the levels of metabolic stress
 C
as the consequence of the ischemic/hypoxic environment (11,154), Pearson and Hussain (13)
suggested that the influence of mechanical tension and metabolic stress may be additive (Figure
A
3). However, the relative contributions of these primary factors are not known. Also, the gains
achieved by combining high-load and low-load exercises with BFR in the same session or in
separate sessions need to be compared with a program of moderate-load strength training with
brief inter-set intervals (such as the 3/7 method). Well-designed studies are needed to investigate
whether it is more effective to optimize the effects of mechanical tension and metabolic stress by
 combining low-load exercise with BFR and high-load strength training or to use a protocol with
moderate loads and brief inter-set intervals to induce a high level of metabolic stress. An
alternative approach, as used by competitive athletes for many years, is to periodize (block
training) complementary methods throughout a long-term training program (2). Here also,
investigations are needed to determine the most appropriate protocol or the best combination of
protocols.
 D
An additional practical criterion that needs to be considered for persons who have time
 EP
constraints, is the benefit to cost ratio (amount of progress relative to the time spent during
training) of the different protocols. This is also critical for well-trained athlete to improve the
 TE
efficacy of their training programs and to limit the risk of overtraining. In this context, the 3/7
protocol is appealing as one bout of a given exercise can be completed in ~1.5 min.
In conclusion, recent studies reporting contradictory findings to our well-established knowledge
have challenged contemporary concepts about strength training. This uncertainty should be used
 C
as an opportunity to advance the field by augmenting our knowledge on the adaptive
 C
neuromuscular mechanisms of strength and power training, and by offering more consistent
guidelines. As the neuromuscular adaptations are modulated by numerous criteria (e.g., age, sex,
A
individual training status and experience, workout volume, number of sessions per week, and
muscle group), much remains to be done to determine the optimal training dose that maximizes
the performance gains achieved by persons with varying characteristics.

 "identityCheck":"The title 'Subjective Wellness, Acute:Chronic Workloads, and Injury Risk in College Football' and the authors (Sampson, Murray, Williams, Sullivan, Fullagar) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title, so the external DOI is used.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",

 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective analysis of one 17-week NCAA Division I football season: 42 players, 1,807 aligned daily workload and wellness records, and 55 noncontact injuries. Injury risk over the next 3 days was very likely higher when the 7:21-day EWMA acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) was 2 SD above (RR 3.05, 90% CI 1.14 to 8.16) or 2 SD below (RR 2.49, 90% CI 1.11 to 5.58) the mean, and wellness showed no clear association with injury.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a single-team, single-season observational analysis, and the authors say the interaction tests were likely underpowered. Only field-based workloads were measured, so the findings cannot separate ACWR effects from unmeasured resistance work, academic stress or positional demands.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the high-ACWR with 'better' soreness result as a reliable warning sign, when it is an exploratory interaction with wide intervals in one team, and it does not supply a validated load threshold.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Sampson JA, Murray A, Williams S, Sullivan A, Fullagar HHK. Subjective wellness, acute:chronic workloads and injury risk in college football. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003000",
   "abstract":"In one season of data from 42 NCAA Division I football players, high and low daily EWMA ACWRs were associated with higher 3-day noncontact injury risk. High ACWRs were also trivially associated with lower self-reported wellness, and the highest-risk group was athletes who reported 'better' soreness on high-ACWR days.",
   "tldr":"Both unusually high and unusually low workload ratios preceded more noncontact injuries in this college squad, so watching for load spikes and drops still makes sense. Self-reported wellness did not predict injury by itself, and a 'feeling good' report after a load spike is not a reason to add more load.",
   "methods":"Retrospective analysis of one season of GPS and accelerometer workload (PlayerLoad) and a three-item daily wellness questionnaire from 42 athletes. Daily 7:21-day EWMA ACWRs were aligned with next-morning wellness, and a generalized linear mixed model with player as a random effect estimated 3-day noncontact injury risk.",
   "findings":"Across 1,807 training-day records, 55 noncontact injuries occurred. Injury risk was very likely higher at ACWRs 2 SD above (RR 3.05) and 2 SD below (RR 2.49) the mean ACWR of 0.91. High ACWR combined with 'better' soreness was likely or very likely riskier than 'normal' soreness (RR 1.64, 90% CI 1.10 to 2.47) and than 'worse' soreness (RR 2.78, 90% CI 1.21 to 6.38). No clear interaction was found for sleep or energy, and no clear injury effect was found for 'better' or 'worse' wellness on its own.",
   "limitations":"The study is one season from one team with 55 injuries, and the authors say the interaction analyses were likely underpowered. The overall wellness interaction results (for example RR 1.52, 90% CI 0.91 to 2.54) have intervals that include 1, although the abstract describes them as likely higher risk, so the abstract overstates them. The authors suggest coaches or players may have changed load after poor wellness reports, which could mask or distort the link, so the results are associations, not causes. Absolute risks stayed below 15% even at the extremes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use EWMA ACWR together with a simple daily wellness check, and treat large swings in load as a reason to review the session plan. Because the highest-risk group was athletes who felt 'better' on high-ACWR days, do not use good self-reported soreness as a reason to add unplanned load. The authors' rule of thumb to avoid day-to-day ACWR changes above 1 SD is practical guidance, not a tested threshold.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports tracking the EWMA ACWR and short-term wellness together and checking planned against actual load before adding intensity. Sudden rises and sudden drops in load both warrant review, and athletes who feel fine after a spike still need the same check.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It examined workload and wellness in a healthy training season, and the discussion's mention of return to play as a high-ACWR scenario was not measured, so it should not be used to set return-to-play load limits."
 }
}

 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review (PRISMA guidelines, protocol not pre-registered) of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus searches to September 2024, with 1,653 studies screened and 184 included, covering 209 neuromuscular profiling outputs from six methods: DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis. Labels such as 'explosive', 'springy', 'stiff' and 'strong/weak' were usually applied by logical inference, the authors found inconsistent definitions and calculations, and only 47 of 184 studies (26%) reported any reliability statistics.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The quality tool was customised by the authors and was not validated, the review was not pre-registered, and the labels were coded interpretively by the review team. Included studies averaged a 'good' quality score (6.1 of 10), with the EUR and RSI groups rated only 'fair', and the labels are the authors' interpretation rather than validated definitions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the review's label list as validated athlete categories, when the authors found the labels are mostly inferred and no consistent cut-off ranges could be set for any method.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Chua KYH, Leahey SR, Lum D, Fahey JT, Buchheit M, Laffer JC, et al. Terminology and interpretation across neuromuscular profiling methods: a systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02330-2",
   "abstract":"This systematic review examined whether the terms used to describe outputs from six neuromuscular profiling methods match what the methods measure. Across 184 included studies, terms such as 'explosive', 'springy', 'stiff' and 'strong/weak' were often applied without consistent definitions, and reliability was rarely reported.",
   "tldr":"Neuromuscular profiling labels such as 'explosive', 'springy' and 'strong' are often inferred rather than measured, and the same metric is labelled differently across studies. Report the actual metric and its components, and do not treat a label as a validated athlete classification.",
   "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus (last search September 2024) for six profiling methods: DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis. Two reviewers screened studies, 184 were included after full-text review, and extracted output values, terms, mechanisms and reliability data were grouped into four themes with a customised quality tool.",
   "findings":"Across 209 method outputs, no common output range could be set for any method, so most studies were grouped by magnitude only. Higher EUR was mostly read as more efficient stretch-shortening cycle function, but two studies read it the opposite way. Labels for RSI and RSImod ('explosive', 'springy', 'stiff', 'strong') were mostly inferred, and the review notes that 'strong' or 'weak' labels were based on isometric peak force from the IMTP rather than on the DSI itself. Only 47 of 184 sources (26%) reported reliability statistics.",
   "limitations":"The synthesis is interpretive, with subjective coding of terms and the authors' own quality tool. The protocol was not pre-registered, the search was limited to English journal articles, and the EUR and RSI study groups scored only 'fair' on quality. Many RSI studies (33 of 72) did not report the constituent jump height and contact time, which limits interpretation. Crossref lists 2026, but the PDF prints only 2025 on the copyright and accepted-date lines, so 2025 is kept.",
   "practicalImplications":"Report the actual neuromuscular metric and its components, such as peak forces for DSI or jump height and contact time for RSI, rather than a single label. Avoid calling athletes 'explosive', 'springy' or 'stiff' unless the underlying measure supports it. Check whether a test has reliability data before acting on a change, and keep jump instructions and calculation methods the same within a team.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the review supports choosing one or two profiling methods that match the quality of interest, and keeping their constituent variables in view when discussing an athlete's profile. Define the terms you use for coaches, and track change within the same test protocol so differences reflect the athlete rather than the method.",
   "rtp":"This review included only healthy participants and does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria. Do not use these profiling labels to judge strength, stiffness or readiness after injury."
 }
}

4	Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling
5	Methods: A Systematic Review
6	Kelvin YH. Chua1 · Samuel R. Leahey1 · Danny Lum2,3 · Jack T. Fahey4 · Martin Buchheit1,5 · Jason C. Laffer1 ·
7	Mackenzie CN. Evans1 · Youssef J. Wannouch1 · Paul Comfort4,6
8	Accepted: 17 September 2025
9	© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025
10	Abstract
11	Background Neuromuscular profiling (NP) provides an objective means of assessing neuromuscular function to guide
12	targeted training interventions. However, coaching terminology used to describe NP outputs (e.g., ‘explosive’, ‘springy’) is
13	often inconsistently defined or applied, leading to misinterpretation and limiting effective use. Variations in how NP metrics
14	are calculated and interpreted further complicate comparisons across studies and practical applications. Despite their wide-
15	spread use in sport science and performance settings, no framework currently exists to evaluate whether the terminology
16	and interpretations associated with NP metrics accurately represent measured outputs and intended neuromuscular traits.
17	Objectives This review aimed to evaluate whether terms/labels used across six commonly applied NP methods—Dynamic
18	Strength Index, Eccentric Utilisation Ratio, Force–Velocity Profile, Impulse Analysis, Reactive Strength Index, and Reactive
19	Strength Index Modified—accurately represent the neuromuscular characteristics they are intended to measure. A second-
20	ary objective was to identify methodological limitations that may affect the interpretation, standardisation, and practical
21	application of these methods.
22	Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus identified 1653 eligible studies, of which 184 met
23	inclusion criteria. A modified quality scale was used to assess study relevance. Extracted data included reported output val-
24	ues, assigned terms/labels, underlying mechanisms, and supporting evidence. Results were grouped by explanatory themes,
25	with terms/labels identified and examined based on the underlying mechanisms they were intended to represent. Findings
26	were then synthesised to identify patterns in terminology, interpretation, and limitations.
27	Results A total of 209 NP methods were evaluated (147 ratio-based, 62 non-ratio-based). NP interpretation was task-depend-
28	ent and influenced by methodological variability. Inconsistency was found in the terminology, definitions, and calculations
29	used to derive NP metrics. Several studies attempted to classify athletes based on NP metrics, though few accounted for
30	constituent components in interpretation. Commonly used terms/labels included: ‘explosive/explosiveness’ (indicating greater
31	rate of force development), ‘spring/springy’ (suggesting effective stretch–shortening cycle utilisation), ‘stiff/compliant’
32	(representing a continuum of lower extremity stiffness), and ‘strong/weak’ (reflecting maximal force production capability).
33	Conclusions This review offers a consolidated synthesis of NP terminology, interpretation, and methodological considera-
34	tions. Clarifying terminology and addressing limitations may improve communication between researchers and practitioners,
35	supporting more standardised use of NP tools.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling
Methods: A Systematic Review
Kelvin YH. Chua1 · Samuel R. Leahey1 · Danny Lum2,3 · Jack T. Fahey4 · Martin Buchheit1,5 · Jason C. Laffer1 ·
Mackenzie CN. Evans1 · Youssef J. Wannouch1 · Paul Comfort4,6
Accepted: 17 September 2025
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025
Abstract
Background Neuromuscular profiling (NP) provides an objective means of assessing neuromuscular function to guide
targeted training interventions. However, coaching terminology used to describe NP outputs (e.g., ‘explosive’, ‘springy’) is
often inconsistently defined or applied, leading to misinterpretation and limiting effective use. Variations in how NP metrics
are calculated and interpreted further complicate comparisons across studies and practical applications. Despite their wide-
spread use in sport science and performance settings, no framework currently exists to evaluate whether the terminology
and interpretations associated with NP metrics accurately represent measured outputs and intended neuromuscular traits.
Objectives This review aimed to evaluate whether terms/labels used across six commonly applied NP methods—Dynamic
Strength Index, Eccentric Utilisation Ratio, Force–Velocity Profile, Impulse Analysis, Reactive Strength Index, and Reactive
Strength Index Modified—accurately represent the neuromuscular characteristics they are intended to measure. A second-
ary objective was to identify methodological limitations that may affect the interpretation, standardisation, and practical
application of these methods.
Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus identified 1653 eligible studies, of which 184 met
inclusion criteria. A modified quality scale was used to assess study relevance. Extracted data included reported output val-
ues, assigned terms/labels, underlying mechanisms, and supporting evidence. Results were grouped by explanatory themes,
with terms/labels identified and examined based on the underlying mechanisms they were intended to represent. Findings
were then synthesised to identify patterns in terminology, interpretation, and limitations.
Results A total of 209 NP methods were evaluated (147 ratio-based, 62 non-ratio-based). NP interpretation was task-depend-
ent and influenced by methodological variability. Inconsistency was found in the terminology, definitions, and calculations
used to derive NP metrics. Several studies attempted to classify athletes based on NP metrics, though few accounted for
constituent components in interpretation. Commonly used terms/labels included: ‘explosive/explosiveness’ (indicating greater
rate of force development), ‘spring/springy’ (suggesting effective stretch–shortening cycle utilisation), ‘stiff/compliant’
(representing a continuum of lower extremity stiffness), and ‘strong/weak’ (reflecting maximal force production capability).
Conclusions This review offers a consolidated synthesis of NP terminology, interpretation, and methodological considera-
tions. Clarifying terminology and addressing limitations may improve communication between researchers and practitioners,
supporting more standardised use of NP tools.

   "abstract":"The limb symmetry index is widely used to judge recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but the evidence supporting it for return-to-sport decisions is mixed.    "tldr":"Do not rely on a single limb symmetry percentage after ACL injury. Pair it with a benchmark that suits the athlete, measure both limbs across several tests and movement strategies, and judge readiness against the sport's demands.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of the scientific literature on limb symmetry and asymmetry indices after ACL reconstruction, with practical considerations drawn from that literature. No systematic search or quantitative synthesis is described.",
   "findings":"The authors argue that the postinjury contralateral limb is a poor default benchmark because ACL injury can reduce its strength and function, which can inflate the LSI. Movement asymmetries are often variable and task-dependent, and a performance-based LSI can hide a different movement strategy, since stronger hip extensors can let an athlete match jump distance while masking knee-extensor weakness. They propose using preinjury or noninjured control benchmarks where available, measuring several tests and movement cycles, and tracking both limbs across a sport-specific envelope of function.",
   "limitations":"No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors state that the evidence on LSI cut-offs and reinjury is mixed, and that longitudinal biomechanical testing and load monitoring for return to sport are in their infancy. Preinjury baseline data and control groups are often unavailable in clinical or community settings, which limits the benchmarks they propose.",
   "practicalImplications":"Keep the LSI as one measure rather than the only return-to-sport criterion. Use preinjury or control benchmarks where data exist, and read the contralateral limb with caution after ACL injury. Test several tasks over several trials and sessions, check reliability for the asymmetry measures you use, and track each limb's own performance over time.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the paper supports tracking both limbs independently across vertical and horizontal jumps, change-of-direction tasks and strength tests, with jump strategy measures such as countermovement and drop-jump kinetics alongside the symmetry ratio. Compare the athlete with the demands of the sport and the planned load, not with a single symmetry percentage.",
   "rtp":"The paper supports a multi-test, both-limb approach to return-to-sport readiness after ACL reconstruction, but it does not supply validated pass or fail thresholds. Do not use it to replace LSI cut-offs such as 85 or 90 percent with a new number, because the envelope-of-function approach has no threshold yet."
 }
