 "evidenceSummary":"Secondary analysis of publicly posted Canadian Football League (CFL) Combine results and draft outcomes (2011 to 2019) for three position groups: line (n = 221), big skill (n = 177) and skill (n = 231). Binary logistic models with repeated cross-validation produced a physical success score for each group, with mean validation AUCs of 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), compared with 0.71, 0.67 and 0.78 for a classification tree benchmark.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The outcome is drafted or not, not performance in the field, and the scores come from one league's past combine selections without external validation. The paper's own AUC figures are inconsistent between sections, so the discrimination estimates are approximate.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a high score or a predicted draft probability as a forecast for an individual player's draft or career, when the model describes past combine selections and omits skill.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Matsuo H, Funasaki K, Yamada S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical success score for the Canadian Football League combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(3):695-701.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004047",
   "abstract":"The authors built a simple scoring system, the physical success score (PSS), from CFL Combine measures to classify draft success for three position groups. Cross-validated logistic models identified the predictors and reference values for each group.",
   "tldr":"Position-specific score tables link combine measures such as height, mass and 40-yard sprint time to draft selection, and show the draft probability for each total score. Use them as reference points for goal setting, not as a prediction for any one player.",
   "methods":"Combine data (40-yard dash, bench press, vertical jump, broad jump, shuttle run, 3-cone drill, height and mass) and binary draft outcome were taken from public CFL records for players in three position groups. Repeated grid-search cross-validation selected predictors for a logistic model, and each measure was scored by category against a base category, with draft probability estimated for every possible total score.",
   "findings":"The final models included height, mass and 40-yard sprint in all groups, with vertical jump in the line group, 3-cone in the line and big skill groups, and bench press in the big skill and skill groups; the 40-yard sprint was significant in all three models. Validation AUCs for the PSS were 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), above the classification tree benchmark (0.71, 0.67 and 0.78). The score tables show, for example, a line total score of 2.0 corresponding to a draft probability of 79.5 to 90.5 percent.",
   "limitations":"The outcome is drafted or not, regardless of round, so it does not measure playing success. The abstract gives 211 line players, while the Methods and Table 4 give 221. The validation AUCs in the Methods (0.81, 0.79 and 0.88) differ from those in the Results (0.77, 0.76 and 0.83), and the model was not tested on independent players. Only complete data were used, and the competition level is not stated beyond draft candidates. The authors describe the scores as reference values for size and athletic ability, not skill.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches can use the position-specific tables to see which combine-style measures (height, mass, 40-yard sprint, and for some groups bench press or 3-cone) relate to draft selection, and what a total score implies. Use the tables as goal reference points and progress markers, since they describe past selections and exclude skill.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff working with gridiron prospects, the tables give position-specific targets for body size, 40-yard speed and strength or agility. The largest gaps between an athlete's results and the target bands show where to focus training, while skill assessment has to be done separately because the scores do not measure it.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It relates combine-day test results to draft selection in prospects and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play."
 }
}

13	 Matsuo, H, Funasaki, K, and Yamada, S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical
14	 success score for the Canadian football league combine. J Strength Cond Res 36(3): 695–701, 2022—In the scouting combine of
15	 the Canadian Football League (CFL), players are measured for 6 athletic abilities, including 2 measurements of body size. For
16	 coaches and their players who desire to play in the CFL, knowing the players metrics that are important for being drafted and their
17	 levels will help coaches plan and evaluate their training. Thus, the purpose of this study was to provide a simple scoring system using
18	 the predictors of CFL Combines identified by multivariate analysis and their regression coefficients, and reference values. In this
19	 study, authors created a scoring system to classify draft success and failure of CFL Combines based on the measurement results.
20	 This scoring system was named as the physical success score (PSS). To do so, a repeated grid-search cross-validation for variable
21	 selection algorithm was performed on the players (line: n 5 211, big skill linebacker, running back and tight end: n 5 177, skill
22	 [defensive back and wide receiver]: n 5 231) who participated in the CFL Combines between 2011 and 2019. The final binary
23	 logistic regression models and the reference values were used to generate the PSS for each group. As a result, PSS of the line, big
24	 skill, and skill were developed. In each group, all possible total scores and the estimated draft success probability were shown. From
25	 the results of this study, it was concluded that the PSS approach can provide useful information for coaches in setting training goals.
26	 Key Words: goal setting of training, multivariate analysis, scoring system

 Abstract
 Matsuo, H, Funasaki, K, and Yamada, S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical
 success score for the Canadian football league combine. J Strength Cond Res 36(3): 695–701, 2022—In the scouting combine of
 the Canadian Football League (CFL), players are measured for 6 athletic abilities, including 2 measurements of body size. For
 coaches and their players who desire to play in the CFL, knowing the players metrics that are important for being drafted and their
 levels will help coaches plan and evaluate their training. Thus, the purpose of this study was to provide a simple scoring system using
 the predictors of CFL Combines identified by multivariate analysis and their regression coefficients, and reference values. In this
 study, authors created a scoring system to classify draft success and failure of CFL Combines based on the measurement results.
 This scoring system was named as the physical success score (PSS). To do so, a repeated grid-search cross-validation for variable
 selection algorithm was performed on the players (line: n 5 211, big skill linebacker, running back and tight end: n 5 177, skill
 [defensive back and wide receiver]: n 5 231) who participated in the CFL Combines between 2011 and 2019. The final binary
 logistic regression models and the reference values were used to generate the PSS for each group. As a result, PSS of the line, big
 skill, and skill were developed. In each group, all possible total scores and the estimated draft success probability were shown. From
 the results of this study, it was concluded that the PSS approach can provide useful information for coaches in setting training goals.
 Key Words: goal setting of training, multivariate analysis, scoring system

 "id":"Q55",
 "sourceFile":"The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults' and authors (Rigney, Dugan, et al.) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI is also printed on the first page.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional online survey of 107 men (mean age 60.6 years) with amateur American football exposure, recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. After adjusting for age, number of concussions and total years of football, starting before age 12 was not a significant predictor of depression, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes (for example PHQ-9 B = 0.51, p = 0.682), while more lifetime concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9, GAD-7, NSI and BC-CCI scores.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is cross-sectional, with retrospective self-reported exposure and symptoms from registry volunteers, so recall bias and selection are likely. The under-12 group was younger (mean 53 versus 65 years), and the authors note that a younger, healthier sample may mask later-life effects, so the null result for age of first exposure is not strong evidence of safety.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null age-of-first-exposure result as proof that early tackle football is harmless, when the study has 41 players in the under-12 group, a mean age of 60, and no measure of when or how the concussions occurred.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Rigney GH, Dugan JE, Bishay A, Jonzzon S, Jo J, Williams KL, et al. The association between age of first exposure to American football at a young age and later-life health issues in healthy, community-dwelling adults. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02239-w",
   "abstract":"In 107 former amateur American football players, starting to play before age 12 was not associated with depressive, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes after adjustment. A greater number of lifetime concussions was associated with worse psychiatric, cognitive and neurobehavioral scores.",
   "tldr":"Among healthy former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life mood, cognition or health scores, but more lifetime concussions were. Use this as evidence that concussion burden matters, not as a green light for early tackling.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey of men with at least one year of amateur American football participation who were recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. Multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, number of lifetime concussions and total years of football for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), and general health, motor and functional outcomes.",
   "findings":"Of 107 analysed men (41 with age of first exposure under 12, 66 with 12 or older), age of first exposure under 12 did not predict PHQ-9 (B = 0.51, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B = 0.09, p = 0.926), NSI (B = -0.56, p = 0.850) or BC-CCI (B = -0.65, p = 0.403). Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001. More concussions were also associated with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted comparisons showed higher PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores and more sleep problems in the under-12 group, but these were not significant after adjustment for age.",
   "limitations":"The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and the dichotomy at age 12 follows prior studies rather than a tested threshold. Other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for, and the authors note the results may differ in older, less healthy or professional players.",
   "practicalImplications":"This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The finding that more lifetime concussions went with worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player and managing head impacts carefully at every age. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance and medical staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history and reviewing it when planning contact load. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001. More concussions were also associated with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted comparisons showed higher PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores and more sleep problems in the under-12 group, but these were not significant after adjustment for age.",
   "limitations":"The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and the dichotomy at age 12 follows prior studies rather than a tested threshold. Other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for, and the authors note the results may differ in older, less healthy or professional players.",
   "practicalImplications":"This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The finding that more lifetime concussions went with worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player and managing head impacts carefully at every age. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance and medical staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history and reviewing it when planning contact load. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."

12	Introduction Younger age of first exposure (AFE) to American Football (football) is associated with later-life health problems
13	among former professional athletes in several studies; however, studies examining amateur (i.e., nonprofessional) athletes
14	are less clear.
15	Objective In a cohort of former amateur American Football players, this study assessed whether AFE to football was associ-
16	ated with: (1) psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptoms, (2) cognitive difficulties, (3) general health problems, (4) motor
17	symptoms, and (5) functional status.
18	Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
19	was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
20	Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
21	ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
22	of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.

24	4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was

26	SE: 0.95, p = 0.926), NSI (B: − 0.56, SE: 2.93, p = 0.850), or BC-CCI (B: − 0.65, SE: 0.77, p = 0.403). However, more prior

28	(B: 1.04, SE: 0.23, p < 0.001), and BC-CCI scores (B: 0.26, SE: 0.06, p < 0.001). AFE < 12 did not predict general health
29	problems or independent functional status.

Abstract
Introduction Younger age of first exposure (AFE) to American Football (football) is associated with later-life health problems
among former professional athletes in several studies; however, studies examining amateur (i.e., nonprofessional) athletes
are less clear.
Objective In a cohort of former amateur American Football players, this study assessed whether AFE to football was associ-
ated with: (1) psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptoms, (2) cognitive difficulties, (3) general health problems, (4) motor
symptoms, and (5) functional status.
Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.
Results In total, 107 male participants with exposure to football (mean age: 60.6 ± 15.1 years) reported an average of
4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was
not a significant predictor of PHQ-9 (unstandardized beta, B: 0.51, standard error, SE: 1.25, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B: 0.09,
SE: 0.95, p = 0.926), NSI (B: − 0.56, SE: 2.93, p = 0.850), or BC-CCI (B: − 0.65, SE: 0.77, p = 0.403). However, more prior
concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9 (B: 0.44, SE: 0.10, p < 0.001), GAD-7 (B: 0.33, SE: 0.07, p < 0.001), NSI
(B: 1.04, SE: 0.23, p < 0.001), and BC-CCI scores (B: 0.26, SE: 0.06, p < 0.001). AFE < 12 did not predict general health
problems or independent functional status.
Conclusions AFE to football was not associated with adverse psychiatric, cognitive, neurobehavioral, or general health
outcomes among young, former amateur American Football players. However, more lifetime concussions were associated
with adverse cognitive and psychiatric health outcomes. Future studies should examine similar outcomes in older cohorts
with more comorbidities to further minimize potential confounding between general health and lack of later-life symptoms.

{
 "id":"Q56",
 "sourceFile":"The deceleration deficit - A novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'The Deceleration Deficit: A Novel Field-Based Method to Quantify Deceleration During Change of Direction Performance' and authors (Clarke, Read, De Ste Croix, Hughes) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title, so the external DOI is used.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Female Athletes","Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional study of 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes (19 women, 17 men; mean age 20.3 years) who completed 505 change-of-direction trials in both turning directions and 15-m sprints in one session. Linear sprint times correlated strongly with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76) but not with the change-of-direction deficit (CODD) or the new deceleration deficit (DD), and DD correlated only moderately with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44) and with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). In 78 percent of athletes, DD and CODD differed by more than a moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a single-session correlational study with no reliability or validity testing of DD, and the authors say those analyses are needed before DD is used with individual athletes. Braking forces were not measured, and the sample's performance level limits generalisation.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat DD as a validated measure of deceleration ability that pinpoints each athlete's limiter, when the paper shows only correlations from one session and calls for reliability and validity work.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Clarke R, Read PJ, De Ste Croix MBA, Hughes JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(9):2434-2439.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003856",
   "abstract":"The study compared a new field-based deceleration deficit (DD) with the established change-of-direction deficit (CODD) and linear sprint speed in 36 athletes. Linear speed was strongly related to 505 time but not to either deficit, while DD was only moderately related to CODD and 505 time.",
   "tldr":"Linear sprint time and CODD both tracked 505 time closely in this sample, while the new deceleration deficit (DD) was only moderately related to it. DD may show braking ability that CODD hides, since the two disagree for most athletes, so check both, per turning direction, before deciding what limits an athlete.",
   "methods":"In one session, 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15-m sprints with timing gates. DD was the 505 approach time minus the 15-m sprint time, and CODD was the 505 time minus the 10-m sprint time. Pearson correlations and z-scores with a moderate worthwhile change threshold compared the measures.",
   "findings":"Linear sprint times correlated with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76), while neither 10-m nor 15-m sprint time was related to CODD or DD. CODD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.74 to 0.77), and DD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44) and with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). A moderate worthwhile change between the two deficit z-scores was seen in 78 percent of athletes in at least one turning direction.",
   "limitations":"The study is a single-session cross-sectional correlation with 36 athletes, and the authors state that the reliability and validity of DD still need testing. No force-plate data were collected, so the braking contribution cannot be measured directly. The paper describes the sample as both recreationally active and competitive university-level, and the authors caution that results may not carry over to other performance levels. The DD correlations with the other measures are all below 0.5, which the authors say accounts for only about 20 percent of DD. The abstract states that linear speed has the strongest relationship with 505 time, but the reported coefficients show CODD at least as strong (r = 0.74 to 0.77 versus 0.71 to 0.76 for linear sprints), so the table values are used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 505 test with a 15-m sprint in the same session to separate linear speed from braking ability, and compare DD with CODD for each turning direction. When the two deficits disagree, the paper suggests CODD alone could misjudge an athlete's deceleration, so look at DD before deciding whether deceleration is the limiter. Because the metric is not yet tested for reliability, use the flag to guide further assessment, not as a fixed training prescription.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports testing linear speed and deceleration separately instead of relying on total 505 time or CODD alone. Look at both turning directions, since the paper shows the two deficits often disagree. Track how athletes respond to any deceleration-focused work, because the paper does not show that training DD changes change-of-direction performance.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested currently uninjured athletes in one session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or change in deceleration after injury. Do not use DD as a return-to-sport or change-of-direction clearance criterion."
 }
}

Look at both turning directions, since the paper shows the two deficits often disagree.  deceleration during change of direction performance. J Strength Cond Res 36(9): 2434–2439, 2022—The study investigated the
 relationship between linear and change of direction (COD) speed performance components and the individual differences between
 deceleration deficit (DD) and COD deficit (CODD). Thirty-six subjects (mean 6 SD: age 5 20.3 6 2.9 years; stature 5 175.2 6 7.7

 cm; and body mass 5 78.0 6 16.7 kg) completed 3 trials of a 505 test in both turning directions (dominant [D]; nondominant [ND])
 and 3 15-m linear sprints. Deceleration deficit was calculated by the 15-m approach in the 505 test, minus the athlete’s linear 15-m
 sprint time. To compare individuals CODD and DD, z-scores were calculated, and moderate worthwhile changes (MWCs) were
 identified between these deficit z-scores. Significant correlations were identified between linear sprints and 505 time (D: r 5 0.71,
 0.74; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.76, 0.75; P , 0.01) for 10-m and 15-m sprint. respectively, and between 505 performance and CODD (D:
 r 5 0.74; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.77; P , 0.01) and DD (D: r 5 0.41, P , 0.05. ND: r 5 0.44, P , 0.01). Deceleration deficit was
 significantly related to CODD (D: r 5 0.59; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.62; P , 0.01); however, 78% of subjects demonstrated differences
 between these deficit measures greater than an MWC. In conclusion, linear speed has the strongest significant relationship with 505
 performance. Deceleration deficit could provide a more isolated construct than CODD which may be related to an athlete’s
 deceleration capabilities.

{
 "id":"Q50",
 "sourceFile":"Strength training - In search of optimal strategies to maximize neuromuscular performance.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'Strength Training: in Search of Optimal Strategies to Maximize Neuromuscular Performance' and authors (Duchateau, Stragier, Baudry, Carpentier) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI 10.1249/JES.0000000000000234 is also printed in the text.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Perspective-style narrative review (no search method is described) comparing high-load strength training with low-load exercise under blood flow restriction (BFR), and summarising meta-analyses that disagree on whether high-load training gives larger strength gains while showing similar hypertrophy. The authors also report their own 3/7 method studies: in a 12-week bench press study in physically active people, 1RM rose 29.8% with 3/7 versus 21.8% with volume-matched 4x6 (p < 0.05), although doubling volume (8x6) gave a larger 1RM gain (35.9%) than 3/7.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a narrative perspective with no described search, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. It relies heavily on the authors' own 3/7 studies, the text does not give their sample sizes, and the authors state that their proposed protocols need more testing.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 3/7 method as a proven superior protocol, when the advantage comes from the authors' own studies in active or moderately trained people, a higher-volume 8x6 protocol gave a larger bench press 1RM gain, and the paper calls for more experiments.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Duchateau J, Stragier S, Baudry S, Carpentier A. Strength training: in search of optimal strategies to maximize neuromuscular performance. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews. 2020. Published ahead of print.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jes.0000000000000234",
   "abstract":"Low-load training under blood-flow restriction (BFR) can increase muscle size and maximal strength about as well as heavy-load training, but it produces only minor neural adaptations. The authors propose protocols that combine high voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.",
   "tldr":"Low-load BFR training builds size and strength but adds little neural adaptation and may not be enough for well-trained athletes. The paper argues for combining high mechanical tension with metabolic stress, for example through brief inter-set rests, but this needs testing in more groups.",
   "methods":"Perspective-style narrative review. The authors compare high-load training with low-load BFR training, discuss the mechanisms of hypertrophy and neural adaptation, summarise meta-analyses, and present their own 3/7 method studies against comparison protocols.",
   "findings":"Two meta-analyses (one in musculoskeletal patients, one in mixed populations) found smaller strength gains with low-load BFR than with high-load training, about 7% smaller in the latter, while a third with stricter inclusion criteria found no difference; hypertrophy differed by less than 1%. In the authors' 12-week elbow flexor study in moderately trained people, the 3/7 method raised 1RM by 22.2% versus 12.1% for 8x6, and biceps thickness by 9.6% versus 5.5%. Low-load BFR training produces only minor neural adaptations, and the mechanisms of its hypertrophy effect remain unresolved.",
   "limitations":"The narrative format means the literature selection cannot be checked, and the paper leans on the authors' own studies, whose sample sizes are not given in the text. In the bench press study, 8x6 produced a larger 1RM gain (35.9%) and peak power gain (21.6% versus 16.3%) than 3/7, so the 3/7 advantage holds only against volume-matched or reverse-order protocols. Figure 3 is a hypothetical model. Crossref lists 2021, but the PDF prints 2020 on the copyright line and marks the article as published ahead of print, so 2020 is kept. No volume or page numbers are printed.",
   "practicalImplications":"Low-load BFR training looks usable for patients and for sedentary or older adults, but the paper judges it likely insufficient for well-trained athletes who need high strength or power. For athletes, the authors suggest alternating high-load and low-load BFR work, using moderate-to-high loads with brief inter-set rests, or periodising complementary methods, and say well-designed studies are still needed to choose between them.",
   "athleteDev":"For strength coaches, the paper suggests that well-trained athletes should not rely on low-load BFR alone for maximal strength. It offers moderate loads (about 70% 1RM) with brief rests (the 3/7 method, about 1.5 min per exercise bout) as a time-efficient option, while noting that a higher-volume 8x6 protocol gave larger 1RM gains in one study. Test any new protocol on your own athletes first, since the 3/7 evidence comes from active and moderately trained people.",
   "rtp":"This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its rehabilitation content is limited to the statement that low-load BFR training is valid and safe for frail and sarcopenic patients, which does not set return-to-play criteria for athletes. Do not use the BFR evidence to set post-injury loading targets for athletes."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "findings: 'a high-load advantage of about 7% appeared in one analysis and not in another' -> two meta-analyses showed smaller BFR strength gains (7% in Lixandrao), one showed none ('One analysis on patients ... and another analysis on various population ... both indicated that the increase in muscle strength was less after low-load exercise training with BFR')",
     "evidenceSummary/limitations/synthesisCaution: added that 8x6 beat 3/7 for bench press 1RM (35.9%) and peak power ('Doubling the number of sets ... slightly increased (p<0.05) the gain in 1RM load (35.9%) compared with the 3/7 method')",
     "practicalImplications: garbled 'combining heavy loads and moderate loads with brief rests' -> the three options the authors list (alternate high-load and low-load BFR, moderate-to-high loads with brief rests, or periodise)",
     "athleteDev: removed 'heavier loads with longer rests' as an authors' recommendation and added the 8x6 caveat"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Year: PDF is the 2020 published-ahead-of-print version (accepted 07/20/2020, copyright 2020); Crossref gives 2021 (issue year). 2020 kept per rule.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q51",
 "sourceFile":"Subjective wellness acute-chronic workloads and injury risk in college football.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'Subjective Wellness, Acute:Chronic Workloads, and Injury Risk in College Football' and the authors (Sampson, Murray, Williams, Sullivan, Fullagar) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title, so the external DOI is used.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective analysis of one 17-week NCAA Division I football season: 42 players, 1,807 aligned daily workload and wellness records, and 55 noncontact injuries. Injury risk over the next 3 days was very likely higher when the 7:21-day EWMA acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) was 2 SD above (RR 3.05, 90% CI 1.14 to 8.16) or 2 SD below (RR 2.49, 90% CI 1.11 to 5.58) the mean, and wellness showed no clear association with injury.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a single-team, single-season observational analysis, and the authors say the interaction tests were likely underpowered. Only field-based workloads were measured, so the findings cannot separate ACWR effects from unmeasured resistance work, academic stress or positional demands.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the high-ACWR with 'better' soreness result as a reliable warning sign, when it is an exploratory interaction with wide intervals in one team, and it does not supply a validated load threshold.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Sampson JA, Murray A, Williams S, Sullivan A, Fullagar HHK. Subjective wellness, acute:chronic workloads and injury risk in college football. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003000",
   "abstract":"In one season of data from 42 NCAA Division I football players, high and low daily EWMA ACWRs were associated with higher 3-day noncontact injury risk. High ACWRs were also trivially associated with lower self-reported wellness, and the highest-risk group was athletes who reported 'better' soreness on high-ACWR days.",
   "tldr":"Both unusually high and unusually low workload ratios preceded more noncontact injuries in this college squad, so watching for load spikes and drops still makes sense. Self-reported wellness did not predict injury by itself, and a 'feeling good' report after a load spike is not a reason to add more load.",
   "methods":"Retrospective analysis of one season of GPS and accelerometer workload (PlayerLoad) and a three-item daily wellness questionnaire from 42 athletes. Daily 7:21-day EWMA ACWRs were aligned with the next day's pre-training wellness, and a generalized linear mixed model with player as a random effect estimated 3-day noncontact injury risk, interpreted with magnitude-based probabilities.",
   "findings":"Across 1,807 training-day records, 55 noncontact injuries occurred. Injury risk was very likely higher at ACWRs 2 SD above (RR 3.05) and 2 SD below (RR 2.49) the mean ACWR of 0.91. High ACWR combined with 'better' soreness was likely or very likely riskier than 'normal' soreness (RR 1.64, 90% CI 1.10 to 2.47) and than 'worse' soreness (RR 2.78, 90% CI 1.21 to 6.38). No clear interaction was found for sleep or energy, and no clear injury effect was found for 'better' or 'worse' wellness on its own.",
   "limitations":"The study is one season from one team with 55 injuries, and the authors say the interaction analyses were likely underpowered. The overall-wellness interaction results (RR 1.52, 90% CI 0.91 to 2.54; RR 2.36, 90% CI 0.83 to 6.74) are labelled 'likely' higher risk under magnitude-based inference in both the abstract and results, although their 90% intervals include 1; the abstract also misprints the upper limit as 674. The authors suggest coaches or players may have changed load after poor wellness reports, so the results are associations, not causes. Absolute risks stayed below 15% even at the extremes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use EWMA ACWR together with a simple daily wellness check, and treat large swings in load as a reason to review the session plan. Because the highest-risk group was athletes who felt 'better' on high-ACWR days, do not use good self-reported soreness as a reason to add unplanned load. The authors' suggestion to avoid daily ACWR fluctuations of more than 1 SD of a player's average is practical guidance, not a tested threshold.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports tracking the EWMA ACWR and short-term wellness together and checking planned against actual load before adding intensity. Sudden rises and sudden drops in load both warrant review, and athletes who feel fine after a spike still need the same check.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It examined workload and wellness in a healthy training season, and the discussion's mention of return to play as a high-ACWR scenario was not measured, so it should not be used to set return-to-play load limits."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "limitations: 'the abstract overstates them' -> both abstract and results label the overall-wellness interactions 'likely' under magnitude-based inference although 90% CIs include 1 ('likely higher risk ... (RR: 1.52, 90% CI: 0.91-2.54)'); added the abstract misprint '0.83 to 674' versus results '0.83-6.74'",
     "methods: 'next-morning wellness' -> wellness reported about 2 hours before the next field session; added magnitude-based inference",
     "practicalImplications: 'day-to-day ACWR changes above 1 SD' -> 'daily fluctuations >1 SD of a player's average'"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Year: the abstract citation line prints '2018' while the running header and copyright print 2019; Crossref gives 2019, so 2019 is kept. Sex of the 42 players is not stated, so no sex tag was added.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q52",
 "sourceFile":"Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling Methods - A Systematic Review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling Methods: A Systematic Review' and authors (Chua, Leahey, Lum, et al.) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI 10.1007/s40279-025-02330-2 is also printed on the first page.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review (PRISMA guidelines, protocol not pre-registered) of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus searches to September 2024: 10,574 records identified, 1,653 assessed for eligibility and 184 included, covering 209 neuromuscular profiling outputs from six methods (DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis). Labels such as 'explosive', 'springy', 'stiff' and 'strong/weak' were often applied by logical inference rather than direct measurement, definitions and calculations were inconsistent, and only 47 of 184 studies (26%) reported any reliability statistics.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The quality tool was customised by the authors and was not validated, the review was not pre-registered, and the labels were coded interpretively by the review team. Included studies averaged a 'good' quality score (6.1 of 10), with the EUR and RSI groups rated only 'fair', and the summary labels are the authors' interpretation rather than validated definitions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the review's label list as validated athlete categories, when the authors say the labels reflect interpretive usage and that common value ranges could not be set for EUR, RSI or RSImod.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Chua KYH, Leahey SR, Lum D, Fahey JT, Buchheit M, Laffer JC, et al. Terminology and interpretation across neuromuscular profiling methods: a systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02330-2",
   "abstract":"This systematic review examined whether the terms used to describe outputs from six neuromuscular profiling methods match what the methods measure. Across 184 included studies, terms such as 'explosive', 'springy', 'stiff' and 'strong/weak' were often applied without consistent definitions, and reliability was rarely reported.",
   "tldr":"Neuromuscular profiling labels such as 'explosive', 'springy' and 'strong' are often inferred rather than measured, and the same metric is labelled differently across studies. Report the actual metric and its components, and do not treat a label as a validated athlete classification.",
   "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus (searched February 2023, updated to September 2024) for six profiling methods: DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis. Two reviewers screened studies, 184 were included after full-text review, and extracted output values, terms, mechanisms and reliability data were grouped into four themes.  "sourceFile":"Testing Limb Symmetry and Asymmetry After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury - 4 Considerations to Increase Its Utility.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'Testing Limb Symmetry and Asymmetry After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: 4 Considerations to Increase Its Utility' and authors (Matthew J. Jordan, Chris Bishop) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title, so the external DOI is used.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review (no search method is described) of the limb symmetry index (LSI) and asymmetry index used after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The authors propose four considerations: choose the benchmark carefully, because the postinjury contralateral limb can itself be affected; treat movement asymmetries as task-dependent and variable; measure task performance and movement strategy alongside the LSI; and assess both limbs against a sport-specific envelope of function.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review has no described search, so the choice of supporting studies cannot be checked, and the authors state that the evidence for the LSI in return-to-sport decisions is mixed. The envelope-of-function approach is presented as a proposal, and the authors say the evidence base for return-to-sport testing is in its infancy.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the four considerations as a validated replacement for LSI cut-offs, when the paper gives no new pass or fail thresholds and calls for future research to test them.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Jordan MJ, Bishop C. Testing limb symmetry and asymmetry after anterior cruciate ligament injury: 4 considerations to increase its utility. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2024;46(4):406-414.",
   "doi":"10.1519/ssc.0000000000000821",
   "abstract":"The limb symmetry index is widely used to judge recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but the evidence supporting it for return-to-sport decisions is mixed. The authors outline four considerations for improving its use, including benchmark choice, task-dependent movement asymmetry, movement strategy, and an envelope-of-function approach.",
   "tldr":"Do not rely on a single limb symmetry percentage after ACL injury. Pair it with a benchmark that suits the athlete, measure both limbs across several tests and movement strategies, and judge readiness against the sport's demands.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of the scientific literature on limb symmetry and asymmetry indices after ACL reconstruction, with practical considerations drawn from that literature. No systematic search or quantitative synthesis is described.",
   "findings":"The authors argue that the postinjury contralateral limb is a poor default benchmark because ACL injury can reduce its strength and function, which can inflate the LSI. Movement asymmetries are often variable and task-dependent, and a performance-based LSI can hide a different movement strategy, since stronger hip extensors can let an athlete match jump distance while masking knee-extensor weakness. They propose using preinjury or noninjured control benchmarks where available, measuring several tests and movement cycles, and tracking both limbs across a sport-specific envelope of function.",
   "limitations":"No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors state that the evidence on LSI cut-offs and reinjury is mixed, and that longitudinal biomechanical testing and load monitoring for return to sport are in their infancy. Preinjury baseline data and control groups are often unavailable in clinical or community settings, which limits the benchmarks they propose.",
   "practicalImplications":"Keep the LSI as one measure rather than the only return-to-sport criterion. Use preinjury or control benchmarks where data exist, and read the contralateral limb with caution after ACL injury. Test several tasks over several trials and sessions, check reliability for the asymmetry measures you use, and track each limb's own performance over time.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the paper supports tracking both limbs independently across vertical and horizontal jumps, change-of-direction tasks and strength tests, with jump strategy measures such as countermovement and drop-jump kinetics alongside the symmetry ratio. Compare the athlete with the demands of the sport and the planned load, not with a single symmetry percentage.",
   "rtp":"The paper supports a multi-test, both-limb approach to return-to-sport readiness after ACL reconstruction, but it does not supply validated pass or fail thresholds. Do not use it to replace LSI cut-offs such as 85 or 90 percent with a new number, because the envelope-of-function approach has no threshold yet."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"VERIFIED",
   "changes":[],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q55",
 "sourceFile":"The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults' and authors (Rigney, Dugan, et al.) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI is also printed on the first page.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional online survey of 107 men (mean age 60.6 years) with past amateur American football exposure, recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. After adjusting for age, number of concussions and total years of football, starting before age 12 was not a significant predictor of depression, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes (for example PHQ-9 B = 0.51, p = 0.682), while more self-reported lifetime concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9, GAD-7, NSI and BC-CCI scores.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is cross-sectional, with retrospective self-reported exposure, concussions and symptoms from registry volunteers, so recall bias and selection are likely. The under-12 group was younger (mean 53 versus 65 years), and the authors note that a younger, healthier, amateur sample may explain the null result, so it is not strong evidence of safety.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null age-of-first-exposure result as proof that early tackle football is harmless, when the study has 41 players in the under-12 group, a mean age of 60, and no record of whether the self-reported concussions happened in football.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Rigney GH, Dugan JE, Bishay A, Jonzzon S, Jo J, Williams KL, et al. The association between age of first exposure to American football at a young age and later-life health issues in healthy, community-dwelling adults. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02239-w",
   "abstract":"In 107 former amateur American football players, starting to play before age 12 was not associated with depressive, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes after adjustment. A greater number of lifetime concussions was associated with worse psychiatric, cognitive and neurobehavioral scores.",
   "tldr":"Among healthy former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life mood, cognition or health scores after adjustment, but more self-reported lifetime concussions were. Use this as evidence that concussion burden matters, not as a green light for early tackling.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey of men with at least one year of amateur American football participation who were recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. Multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, number of lifetime concussions and total years of football for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), and general health, motor and functional outcomes.",
   "findings":"Of 107 analysed men (41 with age of first exposure under 12, 66 with 12 or older), age of first exposure under 12 did not predict PHQ-9 (B = 0.51, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B = 0.09, p = 0.926), NSI (B = -0.56, p = 0.850) or BC-CCI (B = -0.65, p = 0.403), and results were unchanged with age of first exposure as a continuous variable. Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001, and with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted comparisons showed higher PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores, more current depression (29.3% versus 13.6%) and more sleep problems (p = 0.050) in the under-12 group, but these were not significant once age, concussions and years of play were adjusted for.",
   "limitations":"The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for. The text and Table 2 disagree on years of football in the under-12 group (5.0 versus 5.1 years; p = 0.021 versus p < 0.001), the Table 1 concussion counts for the under-12 group do not add up to 41, and the abstract conclusion calls the sample 'young' despite a mean age of 60.6; table values are reported here.",
   "practicalImplications":"This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The association between more lifetime concussions and worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.",
   "athleteDev":"For medical and performance staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "populations: removed 'Male Athletes' and 'Healthy Athletes' -> 'Adult / Recreational' only; the sample is community-dwelling registry adults (mean age 60.6) with past amateur football, not current athletes",
     "findings: unadjusted differences said to lose significance 'after adjustment for age' -> after adjustment for age, concussions and years of play; added current depression 29.3% vs 13.6% (p = 0.048) and the continuous-AFE sensitivity analysis",
     "limitations: added internal conflicts (text 'p = 0.021' vs Table 2 't = -3.76, p < 0.001' for years of football; Table 1 under-12 concussion counts inconsistent; abstract 'young' vs mean age 60.6); removed the 'dichotomy at age 12' point, since the continuous analysis gave the same result",
     "synthesisCaution: 'no measure of when ... the concussions occurred' -> date of most recent concussion was collected; the gap is that concussions were not tied to football",
     "practicalImplications/athleteDev: removed 'managing head impacts at every age' and 'reviewing history when planning contact load', which the findings do not test"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Clinically sensitive (concussion, youth tackle football). Table 1 concussion distribution for the AFE < 12 column appears garbled in the PDF; check against the published table.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional study of 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes (19 women, 17 men; mean age 20.3 years) who completed 505 change-of-direction trials in both turning directions and 15-m sprints in one session. Linear sprint times correlated strongly with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76) but not with the change-of-direction deficit (CODD) or the new deceleration deficit (DD); DD correlated moderately with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44) and largely with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). In 78 percent of athletes, DD and CODD z-scores differed by more than a moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a single-session correlational study with no reliability or validity testing of DD, and the authors say those analyses are needed before DD is used with individual athletes. Braking forces were not measured, and the sample's performance level limits generalisation.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat DD as a validated measure of deceleration ability that pinpoints each athlete's limiter, when the paper shows only correlations from one session and calls for reliability and validity work.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Clarke R, Read PJ, De Ste Croix MBA, Hughes JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(9):2434-2439.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003856",
   "abstract":"The study compared a new field-based deceleration deficit (DD) with the established change-of-direction deficit (CODD) and linear sprint speed in 36 athletes. Linear speed was strongly related to 505 time but not to either deficit, while DD was moderately related to 505 time and more strongly to CODD.",
   "tldr":"Linear sprint time and CODD both tracked 505 time closely in this sample, while the new deceleration deficit (DD) was only moderately related to it. DD may show braking ability that CODD hides, since the two disagree for most athletes, so check both, per turning direction, before deciding what limits an athlete.",
   "methods":"In one session, 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15-m sprints with timing gates and a contact mat at the turn. DD was the 505 full-approach time (to mid plant-step contact) minus the 15-m sprint time, and CODD was the 505 time minus the 10-m sprint time. Pearson correlations and z-score differences against a moderate worthwhile change (0.5 x between-subject SD) compared the measures.",
   "findings":"Linear sprint times correlated with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76), while neither 10-m nor 15-m sprint time was related to CODD or DD. CODD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.74 to 0.77), and DD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44), with full approach time (r = 0.43 to 0.54) and with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). A moderate worthwhile change between the two deficit z-scores was seen in 78 percent of athletes (28 of 36) in at least one turning direction.",
   "limitations":"The study is a single-session cross-sectional correlation with 36 athletes, and the authors state that the reliability and validity of DD still need testing; without reliability data, some of the DD versus CODD divergence may reflect measurement error. No force-plate data were collected, so the braking contribution cannot be measured directly. The paper describes the sample as both recreationally active and competitive university-level. The authors state that all DD correlations were below r = 0.5, but their tables show r = 0.59 to 0.62 with CODD and 0.54 with full approach in the nondominant direction, and the abstract's claim that linear speed has the strongest relationship with 505 time is not supported by the tables (CODD r = 0.74 to 0.77, full approach r = 0.86 to 0.87); table values are used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 505 test with a 15-m sprint in the same session to separate linear speed from braking ability, and compare DD with CODD for each turning direction. When the two deficits disagree, the paper suggests CODD alone could misjudge an athlete's deceleration, so look at DD before deciding whether deceleration is the limiter. Because the metric is not yet tested for reliability, use the flag to guide further assessment, not as a fixed training prescription.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports testing linear speed and deceleration separately instead of relying on total 505 time or CODD alone. Look at both turning directions, since the paper shows the two deficits often disagree. Track how athletes respond to any deceleration-focused work, because the paper does not show that training DD changes change-of-direction performance.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested currently uninjured athletes in one session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or change in deceleration after injury. Do not use DD as a return-to-sport or change-of-direction clearance criterion."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "limitations: repeated the authors' claim that DD correlations 'are all below 0.5' -> tables show DD vs CODD r = 0.59/0.62 and vs full approach r = 0.54 (ND) (Tables 3 and 4); conflict now stated",
     "limitations: abstract-vs-table conflict extended to note full approach correlates most strongly with 505 (r = 0.86/0.87)",
     "evidenceSummary/abstract: DD-CODD relation 'only moderately' -> 'large' per the paper's scale (0.5-0.7 large)",
     "findings: added DD vs full approach r and the 28 of 36 count (12 + 15 + 1)",
     "limitations: added that divergence may partly reflect unmeasured measurement error, since DD reliability was not tested"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

content.text:
I've written all 8 files to `verified/` and they all parse as valid JSON. Every paper matches its Crossref title, so all keep their external DOI, all stay INCLUDE, and no decision changed. The second-opinion reviewer was rate-limited, so nobody else has checked these corrections.

- **Q49**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Fixed participant counts per step (19 sorted, 20 rated importance, 19 rated confidence) and noted a tie for highest confidence rating. The PDF is a pre-issue proof printing 2021; Crossref says 2022. I kept 2021.
- **Q50**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Two of three meta-analyses favoured high-load training for strength, not one. Added that 8x6 beat the authors' 3/7 method for bench press 1RM (35.9%) and peak power. The PDF is the 2020 ahead-of-print version; Crossref says 2021.
- **Q51**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft said the abstract overstated the wellness results. In fact the abstract and results both call them "likely" higher risk although their 90% intervals include 1. Also flagged an abstract misprint (674 for 6.74) and a 2018 vs 2019 year conflict inside the PDF; I kept 2019.
- **Q52**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. 1,653 studies were assessed in full text, not screened; 10,574 records were found. DSI does have a value range (0.46 to 0.92); only EUR, RSI and RSImod lack one. Labels are "often" inferred rather than "mostly". The PDF says 2025; Crossref says 2026.
- **Q53**: INCLUDE, VERIFIED, high. No errors found. Marked high only because ACL return-to-play testing is clinically sensitive.
